chart_gl.title: Accounts 1 — The Chart of Accounts & the General Ledger
chart_gl.desc: The Accounting workspace foundation: GL Entries and the View > Accounting Ledger button, reading the debit/credit columns, building the Chart of Accounts tree with Add Child and the reading test, the Account Type field and the Company record's default accounts, the posting map document by document with the Stock Received But Not Billed diagnostic, the General Ledger and Trial Balance reports with the monthly scan, and the Receivable/Payable party ledgers with the tie check.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Accounting workspace and the General Ledger
lessons.html:
Open the Accounting workspace. This is the module you will operate for the whole track: the Chart of Accounts, the ledgers and reports, the journal and payment documents, and the settings that govern them. This first module covers the foundation — the Chart of Accounts and the General Ledger — and how to read both.

What a GL Entry is. Every financial event in ZhiftERP is stored as one or more GL Entry rows: posting date, account, debit or credit amount, party where applicable, cost centre, and — always — the voucher: the document that created the row. GL Entries are never edited. Corrections are new entries posted beside the old ones (module 2 covers the procedure). You will not usually open GL Entry records directly; you read them through the General Ledger report (Chapter 6).

The books are written by documents. In ZhiftERP you do not type ledger entries for trading. The trading documents post their own accounting the moment they are submitted:

• Submitting a Sales Invoice posts the revenue, the VAT, and the customer's debt.
• Submitting a Purchase Receipt posts the stock value and the accrual for unbilled goods.
• Submitting a Payment Entry posts the bank movement and clears the debt.

To see this on any submitted document, open it and use the View > Accounting Ledger button: the exact GL rows the document wrote, on one screen. Use this button constantly — it is the fastest teacher in the module.

What this changes about the work. Because documents write the books, the accounts job in ZhiftERP is governing the machine, not typing entries: getting the Chart of Accounts right (Chapters 3-4), knowing what each document posts (Chapter 5), reading the ledger and its reports (Chapters 6-7), and keeping the few genuine manual entries under control (module 2). A business that types Journal Entries for its sales while the Sales Invoice sits unused has switched the system off while paying for it; module 2 covers how to recognise and reverse that habit.

Module contents. Chapter 2: debits and credits — how to read the two amount columns on every ledger screen. Chapter 3: the Chart of Accounts tree — creating and organising accounts. Chapter 4: the Account Type field and the company default accounts. Chapter 5: the posting map — what each document writes. Chapter 6: the General Ledger and Trial Balance reports. Chapter 7: Receivable and Payable accounts and the party ledgers. Chapter 8: the case — HealthTrade, the pharmaceutical distributor this track follows, setting up its chart. Chapter 9: review and the module's law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Debits and credits: reading the ledger columns
lessons.html:
Every ledger screen in ZhiftERP — the General Ledger report, the Accounting Ledger view, the Journal Entry rows — shows two amount columns: Debit and Credit. Learn the direction table once and every screen becomes readable.

The direction table.

• Assets (bank, debtors, stock, equipment) — debit to increase, credit to decrease.
• Expenses (rent, salaries, COGS) — debit to increase.
• Liabilities (creditors, VAT payable, loans) — credit to increase.
• Income (sales) — credit to increase.
• Equity (capital, retained earnings) — credit to increase.

Mnemonic: DEAD — Debits increase Expenses, Assets, Drawings; everything else grows by credit. Every document's rows balance: total debits equal total credits, always. The system enforces this; you never see an unbalanced posting.

Three documents, read on screen. Post these in a test company and open View > Accounting Ledger on each:

1. A Sales Invoice for ₦107,500 (₦100,000 + 7.5% VAT): Debtors debited ₦107,500 (the customer now owes it), Sales credited ₦100,000 (income), VAT Payable credited ₦7,500 (money held for FIRS, not income — module 5 covers the tax accounts).
2. The customer's Payment Entry: Bank debited ₦107,500, Debtors credited ₦107,500 — the debt became cash.
3. A Purchase Receipt at ₦940,000: Stock In Hand debited ₦940,000, Stock Received But Not Billed credited ₦940,000 — the system records that you hold goods you have not yet been billed for. Chapter 5 completes this thread when the Purchase Invoice arrives.

Three reads the table gives you.

• The wrong-side balance. Each account normally carries one side. A customer showing a credit balance in the Accounts Receivable report means you owe them — usually a payment that was never allocated to its invoices. Wrong-side balances are always worth opening.
• The growth read. Credits growing a Sales account is trade; debits growing it are returns and credit notes — check them when large.
• The other side. Every posting has a counterpart row. When an entry looks wrong in the General Ledger report, find its voucher and open the Accounting Ledger view — the counterpart row usually names the mistake.

Practical rule: when a balance confuses you, say it in the table's terms — which account, which side, grew by what — then open the entries. Confusion rarely survives the two steps.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The Chart of Accounts screen
lessons.html:
Open Accounting > Chart of Accounts. The screen shows a tree: bold rows are group accounts (folders for reading), and the rest are ledger accounts — the leaves that take postings. Posting to a group is refused by the system. This chapter is how to build and maintain the tree.

Creating an account. Hover a group row and click Add Child. The dialog asks for:

• Account Name — plain language that will read well in every report for years: Generator Running Costs, not Misc Exp 2.
• Account Number — optional; use it if the business's reporting tradition numbers accounts. Keep gaps for insertion and never reuse a number.
• Is Group — tick to create a folder; leave clear for a posting account. A group cannot take postings; a leaf cannot have children. To convert one to the other later, the account must have no entries.
• Account Type — Chapter 4; the field that wires the account into the machinery.

Every account belongs to one of the fixed root types — Asset, Liability, Equity, Income, Expense — inherited from its position in the tree.

Design from the reading, not the listing. The default chart the setup wizard installs is a workable skeleton. Tailor it in one sitting:

1. Write down the owner's monthly questions — what did we make, what did it cost, where did the money go. These define the income and expense groups.
2. Add what the statements and the audit need. These define the balance-sheet shape.
3. Apply the reading test to every proposed account: an account earns its existence when someone will read its line separately. Three bank accounts are three leaves because three reconciliations will happen. Eleven micro-splits of office expenses that nobody reads separately are clutter — collapse them.

Accounts versus dimensions. Do not create Rent - Ibadan, Rent - Akure. Branch and line distinctions belong in the Cost Center field on postings (module 6), not in account names. One account, Rent; the branch is a filter. The test: opening a new branch should not add a single account.

Maintaining the tree.

• Renaming is safe: open the account and use Rename — history follows the account.
• Moving or merging accounts changes how history reads: plan it, do it at a period boundary, document it. The Chart of Accounts screen allows drag-free re-parenting through the account's Parent Account field.
• Keep creation rights narrow. New accounts are proposed against the reading test, not created per whim. Chapter 9's sprawl pattern is what unrestricted creation produces.

Practical rule: finish the design sitting with the one-line test — every leaf has a one-sentence answer to who reads this line and why. Retire any account that fails it.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Account Type and the company defaults
lessons.html:
Two accounts can sit side by side in the tree and behave completely differently, because of one field: Account Type. Names are for people; the type is what the machinery reads.

The types that matter, and what each switches on.

• Bank and Cash — the account joins the payment machinery: Modes of Payment can point at it, and Bank-type accounts appear in the Bank Reconciliation tool (module 3). A real bank account created without the Bank type is invisible to the reconciliation that proves it.
• Receivable and Payable — every posting to the account requires a Party (Customer or Supplier). This is what creates the per-party ledgers and the Accounts Receivable / Accounts Payable reports (Chapter 7). An invoice pointed at a non-Receivable account leaves the machinery that ages balances and prints statements.
• Stock — reserved for the perpetual-inventory postings: Stock In Hand, Stock Received But Not Billed, the adjustment accounts. The system blocks Journal Entries against Stock-type accounts while perpetual inventory is on (module 2, Chapter 6 explains why).
• Tax — the VAT and WHT accounts the tax templates post to; typed so the tax reports can find them.
• Fixed Asset, Depreciation, Accumulated Depreciation — the asset module's accounts (module 7).
• Round Off and Temporary — the system's designated accounts for rounding differences and opening balances.

The company defaults. Open the Company record (Accounting > Company) and review its account defaults: Default Receivable Account, Default Payable Account, Default Cash and Bank Accounts, Round Off Account and Cost Center, Exchange Gain/Loss Account, Stock Received But Not Billed, Stock Adjustment Account, and the rest. Every document that does not name an account explicitly falls back to these. A wrong default mis-posts every document that relies on it, silently, from day one. Verify the defaults at setup and re-verify after any chart restructuring.

Three working rules.

1. Set the type at creation. Retyping an account that has history is a serious event — a receivable that spent a year untyped has a year of party-less entries no toggle repairs.
2. When a posting misbehaves, check the type first. The invoice that refuses a Party, the bank missing from the reconciliation list — open the account record and read its Account Type before touching anything else.
3. Audit the types annually. Every Bank-type account against the real bank list; the Receivable/Payable accounts against the company defaults; the Round Off account against its intended leaf. Thirty minutes; it removes the whole class of rule-2 errors.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The posting map: what each document writes
lessons.html:
This chapter is the reference card for the track: exactly which GL rows each document posts on submit. Verify each one in a test company with View > Accounting Ledger.

Sales Invoice. Debit Debtors (with the Customer as Party) for the gross; credit the income account per row; credit the tax accounts per the Sales Taxes and Charges template. If Update Stock is ticked (the POS-style flow), the invoice also does the delivery's work: credit Stock In Hand, debit Cost of Goods Sold.

Delivery Note. Credit Stock In Hand at the item's valuation rate; debit Cost of Goods Sold. No revenue posts here. Delivery moves value; invoicing books revenue — and for this reason a period needs both its deliveries and its invoices in before its margin is true (module 7's cut-off).

Payment Entry (Receive). Debit the bank or cash account (from the Mode of Payment); credit Debtors with the Party, allocated against invoices in the References table. Deductions ride in the same entry's Deductions table — WHT withheld by the customer debits the WHT receivable account there (module 5).

Purchase Receipt. Debit Stock In Hand at valuation (rate plus landed costs); credit Stock Received But Not Billed — the accrual that records goods held but not yet billed. Diagnostic worth memorising: the SRBNB account's balance is the queue of receipts awaiting purchase invoices, in naira. If it is old and large, invoices are not being processed.

Purchase Invoice. Credit Creditors (with the Supplier as Party); debit Stock Received But Not Billed, clearing the accrual; debit the input-VAT account per the taxes template. A service invoice with no receipt debits the expense account directly. WHT you deduct from the supplier is applied through the Tax Withholding Category and posts to WHT Payable when the invoice or payment is processed (module 5).

Stock Entry. Material Issue: credit Stock In Hand, debit the expense account named on the entry. Material Receipt: debit Stock In Hand, credit the difference account. Material Transfer: stock accounts only — nothing touches the P&L.

Stock Reconciliation. Debit or credit Stock In Hand against the adjustment account set on the entry — the count difference landing in the P&L where policy directed it.

Journal Entry. Whatever its rows say — which is exactly why module 2 exists.

Three ways to use the map.

1. Verify it live at setup. Post one small real document of each kind; read the Accounting Ledger view against this chapter. A wrong default or template is caught in an hour instead of inherited by a month.
2. Diagnose backwards. A strange GL row names its voucher; the map says what that document should have written; the difference locates the fault.
3. Answer forwards. "Why did this account move?" — the map names the documents that write it; the General Ledger report filtered by account lists the period's instances.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The General Ledger and Trial Balance reports
lessons.html:
Two reports carry most of the reading in this track. Learn their filters and the drill-down and every accounts question becomes a lookup.

The General Ledger report (Accounting > General Ledger). The filters that matter:

• Company / From Date / To Date — always set first. The report shows the opening balance, every entry in range, and the closing balance.
• Account — one account's full story: use it for "how did this balance get here".
• Party Type + Party — one customer or supplier across accounts: their statement on screen.
• Voucher No — one document's complete footprint: the posting map, verified live.
• Group By — Group by Voucher to read documents; Group by Account to read balances.
• Cost Center and dimension filters — module 6's lenses.

The drill-down. Every number in every financial report links downward: statement line → account → GL rows → the voucher → its attachments. Click through it rather than exporting: the disputed figure is opened live in the meeting; the strange balance is walked to its documents the same day. Teach this habit in the first month — a business whose managers drill down argues from documents.

The Trial Balance report (Accounting > Trial Balance). One row per account: opening debit/credit, period debit and credit, closing balance. It always balances — the posting engine guarantees it — so read it for anomalies, not for its total:

1. Accounts that should be zero and are not — Stock Received But Not Billed aging (unprocessed purchase invoices), a temporary or suspense account with residents, a Round Off account trending upward (a symptom, not rounding).
2. Balances on the wrong side — a credit-balance customer (an unallocated payment), a debit-balance VAT Payable.
3. Accounts nobody recognises — Chapter 9's pattern; investigate to the entries, then merge, retire, or document.

The monthly scan, as a procedure.

1. Run the Trial Balance for the month.
2. Flag the three anomaly kinds above.
3. For each flag, open the General Ledger report filtered to that account and read the entries to their vouchers.
4. Fix what has a fix (allocation, correction by module 2's rules) and note what needs a decision.

Ten minutes when done monthly. It is the reason the year-end close (module 7) holds no surprises.

Practical rule: never leave a wrong-side balance or an unexplained account for the close to find. The voucher that explains it is four clicks away today and an excavation in six months.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Receivable and Payable accounts: the party ledgers
lessons.html:
Debtors is one account in the chart, but because every posting to it carries a Party (Chapter 4's type rule), the system maintains a ledger per customer inside it. This chapter is that structure and the check that keeps it trustworthy.

The three faces of the same entries.

• The General Ledger report filtered by Party is the customer's statement — every invoice, payment and credit note in one run.
• The Accounts Receivable report (Accounting > Accounts Receivable) ages every customer's open items into buckets — the collections worklist. Accounts Payable mirrors it for suppliers.
• The Debtors account balance in the Trial Balance is, by construction, the sum of the parties' balances.

The pattern: the control account is the total; the parties are the detail; they agree because they are the same GL rows read three ways.

How the agreement breaks. The tie holds automatically until someone posts around it:

• A Journal Entry row against Debtors without a Party — the system requires a Party on Receivable/Payable accounts, but imported entries, migrations, and permission overrides can slip past. The result: naira in the control that belong to no customer; the AR report's total no longer equals the account.
• A balance "corrected" at the account level while the party detail stands.
• A migration that loaded one opening total per control instead of per-party, per-invoice detail (module 4 covers the loading rules).

The monthly tie check, as a procedure.

1. Run the Trial Balance; note the Debtors closing balance.
2. Run the Accounts Receivable report as at the same date; note its grand total.
3. They must agree to the kobo. Repeat for Creditors against Accounts Payable.
4. On any difference: run the General Ledger report on the control account filtered to Voucher Type = Journal Entry. The offending entry is almost always there, in minutes.

What an intact tie buys. The ageing report is believed, so collections and the payment run work from it. Customer statements print from the party ledger without fear. The auditor samples parties, finds the control every time, and the confirmation exercise ends early. The balance sheet's receivables line is a total with hundreds of defensible components.

Practical rule: the allocation habits taught at the sales and purchasing desks — payments allocated to invoices in the References table, credit notes applied, advances matched — are all tie maintenance from this chair. Module 4 turns them into a standing monthly routine.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's chart is born
lessons.html:
HealthTrade is the pharmaceutical distributor this track follows — three branches, an in-house accountant, a new ZhiftERP system. This chapter is the afternoon its chart was set up, using Chapters 1-7 in order.

Step 1 — the reading list (Chapter 3). Before touching the tree, the MD's monthly questions are written down: sales and margin (eventually by branch — noted for module 6), the running costs read separately (rent, people, power, logistics), and the balance-sheet picture (banks by account, stock, debtors, creditors, the tax accounts). The accountant adds the statement and audit needs. Fifteen questions become the chart's specification.

Step 2 — tailoring the tree (Chapters 3-4). On the Chart of Accounts screen, against the list:

• Three real banks become three Bank-type leaves under Bank Accounts, named with bank and account identity: GTB Current - 0123 style — three reconciliations coming in module 3.
• Debtors and Creditors confirmed as the typed control accounts, and the Company record's defaults walked: Default Receivable and Payable, Round Off Account, Stock Received But Not Billed — two are corrected on the spot (the Round Off account pointed at a proper leaf, and one Mode of Payment mapped to the wrong bank).
• The tax accounts named plainly: VAT Payable, Input VAT, WHT Payable, WHT Receivable — all typed Tax.
• Eleven micro-splits of administrative expenses collapsed to four lines someone will actually read.
• The branch question answered the right way: no per-branch account copies; the branch will be a Cost Center (module 6). One chart, one language.

Step 3 — the posting map verified live (Chapter 5). One small real document of each kind is posted and its View > Accounting Ledger read against the map: a test invoice (Debtors gross, Sales net, VAT Payable — the ₦107,500 pattern read aloud), a Purchase Receipt (the SRBNB accrual explained: this balance is your unbilled receipts queue — watch it clear when the invoice books), a delivery's COGS row tied to the valuation rate, a Payment Entry allocated in its References table and re-read in the party ledger. The hour does what Chapter 5 promises: the wrong defaults are caught before a month inherits them.

Step 4 — the first reads (Chapters 6-7). The drill-down is demonstrated: statement line → account → GL rows → voucher, four clicks. The first Trial Balance scan finds one anomaly — a small credit balance on a customer — drilled in the General Ledger report to an unallocated go-live payment, allocated the same day through Payment Reconciliation. Two monthly routines are diarised: the ten-minute Trial Balance scan, and the tie check (Trial Balance Debtors against the AR report total, to the kobo). The accountant's note at the end of the afternoon: the chart answers my questions instead of the software's.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the first law
lessons.html:
The recurring chart-and-ledger failures. Symptom, cause, fix — then the review list.

Pattern 1 — chart sprawl. Symptom: four hundred accounts for an eleven-person business; every report a scroll; nobody can say what half the accounts are for. Cause: accounts created per whim — one per project, branch, or mood (Chapter 3). Fix: a consolidation sitting — balances merged by documented entries into accounts that are read, unused accounts disabled, creation rights narrowed, and the branch/line distinctions moved to Cost Centers.

Pattern 2 — the suspense squatter. Symptom: a suspense or miscellaneous account with a large, aging, growing balance. Cause: the parking account used as a destination for everything unclassified (Chapters 3, 6). Fix: suspense swept to zero monthly as a close-checklist line, each item classified to its true account, and the source gaps fixed — a default, a template, or training.

Pattern 3 — the untyped account. Symptom: a bank missing from the Bank Reconciliation tool; an invoice refusing a Party; receivables that cannot age. Cause: accounts created with names but without the right Account Type (Chapter 4). Fix: type at creation as a rule, retyping-with-history treated as the serious event it is, and the annual type audit.

Pattern 4 — the party-less posting. Symptom: the Trial Balance's Debtors figure disagreeing with the Accounts Receivable report's total. Cause: entries posted to control accounts without a Party — imports, migrations, permission overrides (Chapter 7). Fix: reconcile the divergence once (the Journal Entry filter finds it), install module 2's journal rules, and run the monthly tie check afterwards.

Pattern 5 — the account nobody can explain. Symptom: the Trial Balance line that draws blank looks in the meeting. Cause: the chart accumulated instead of designed (Chapter 3). Fix: the annual chart walk — each unexplained account read to its entries in the General Ledger report, then merged, disabled, or documented. Deliverable: every line has its one-sentence explanation.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the direction table and DEAD; read the three worked documents from Chapter 2 in the Accounting Ledger view; state the reading test and the account-versus-dimension rule; name the Account Types and what each switches on, and where the company defaults live; recite the posting map document by document, including the SRBNB diagnostic; run the General Ledger report by account, party, and voucher, and the monthly Trial Balance scan; and perform the tie check with its Journal Entry filter.

The first law: the books are written by documents, into a chart designed for reading. Module 2 opens the one document that writes the ledger directly — the Journal Entry — and the rules that keep it safe.

journal_entries.title: Accounts 2 — Journal Entries & the Manual Layer
journal_entries.desc: The Journal Entry doctype: what it bypasses, the form field by field (Entry Type, the Accounting Entries table, the Difference field, References, User Remark), the lawful list with the document and evidence tests, prepayments by Auto Repeat and accruals by Reverse Journal Entry, the four correction rules with Cancel/Amend and the note machinery, the forbidden list with the system's own fences, and the controls — Role Permissions, Workflow thresholds, templates, the five-question monthly review.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Journal Entry doctype
lessons.html:
Open Accounting > Journal Entry > New. This is the one document whose job is writing the General Ledger directly — any accounts, any amounts, whatever its rows say. It exists because real accounting needs it monthly (Chapter 3 lists the lawful uses). It is dangerous because of what it bypasses. This module teaches the form, the uses, and the fences.

What the Journal Entry bypasses. Every trading document carries machinery around its GL posting:

• The Sales Invoice maintains the party ledger, feeds the tax registers, and ages into the Accounts Receivable report.
• The Purchase Receipt writes the stock ledger beside the money.
• The Payment Entry allocates against invoices in its References table.

The Journal Entry carries none of that. It writes bare GL rows. Every naira it posts has skipped the systems that make totals decomposable — the party tie, the stock-to-accounts agreement, the tax registers, the payment allocation. That is not a flaw: the Journal Entry is specialised for events that have no trading document (rent accruing, depreciation charging). But used where a document exists, it fixes the GL's number while breaking every detail beneath it — silently. The Trial Balance still balances; the statements still print; the damage surfaces weeks later as a tie check that will not agree.

The module's rule, stated now. The journal is the exception and the document is the rule: what a document can do, a document must do. Sales are invoiced. Purchases are billed. Stock moves by stock documents. Payments are Payment Entries. The Journal Entry takes what remains — Chapter 3's list, under Chapter 7's controls.

The habit to watch for. Accountants trained on manual books often journalise everything — some systems in the wild are a GL with thousands of Journal Entries and no trading documents at all. The fix is transferring the fluency, not deriding it: each recurring journal examined for the document that should replace it, corrections routed through Chapter 5's procedures, and the monthly Journal Entry count watched as a health figure — open the Journal Entry list, filter by month, read the number. Lawful traffic at a trading business is small; a large or growing count is itself a finding.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the form, field by field. Chapter 3: the lawful list. Chapter 4: accruals and prepayments, with the exact procedures. Chapter 5: corrections. Chapter 6: the forbidden list and the system's fences. Chapter 7: permissions, templates, and the monthly review. Chapter 8: HealthTrade's manual layer. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Journal Entry form, field by field
lessons.html:
The controls in this module live in the form's own fields. Walk them in order on a new Journal Entry.

Entry Type. The first field: Journal Entry, Bank Entry, Cash Entry, Credit Note, Debit Note, Contra Entry, Depreciation Entry, and others. The type does two jobs: some machinery work (Contra Entries are how movements between your own bank and cash accounts are recorded — module 3 uses them), and review work — the monthly review filters by type, and a Bank Entry saved as a plain Journal Entry hides from its reviewer. Choose it correctly every time.

Posting Date. When the entry speaks. Rules: honest dates always (the March accrual is dated in March); closed periods are respected (the freeze settings in module 8 block postings into sealed months); and accrual reversals are dated the 1st of the following month (Chapter 4's procedure).

The Accounting Entries table. One row per account touched:

• Account — a leaf account; the system refuses groups.
• Party Type / Party — mandatory when the account is Receivable or Payable type. The form will not save a Debtors row without its Customer.
• Debit / Credit — one side per row.
• Cost Center — required on income and expense rows once module 6's validation is on. An expense journal must still say whose expense.
• Reference Type / Name — when a row settles against an existing invoice, name it here so the allocation lands.

The Difference field. Below the table, the form shows total debit, total credit, and the difference. The entry will not submit until the difference is zero. A journal that seems to need one side only is a misdiagnosis — the other side exists and has not been found. Parking the difference in a suspense account is not the answer (Chapter 9, Pattern 2).

Reference Number and Reference Date. The external anchor: the bank advice, the payroll summary, the agreement clause. Fill them whenever such paper exists — module 3 requires them on every Bank Entry.

User Remark. The story field, and the most strictly enforced rule in this module: every Journal Entry narrates itself — what happened, why this entry, what evidence supports it. Trading documents are their own explanation; a journal's explanation lives only here. A journal with an empty remark is unusable six months later — nobody, including its author, can say why it exists. No exceptions; templates (Chapter 7) carry their remarks pre-written, so routine traffic costs nothing.

Summary. Correct Entry Type, honest Posting Date, rows with parties and cost centres, references named where rows settle documents, the Difference at zero, external references attached, and a story in User Remark — every time.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The lawful list
lessons.html:
The discipline only holds if the lawful uses are named rather than negotiated case by case. This is the list — a trading business's legitimate Journal Entry traffic:

1. Accruals and prepayments. Expenses spread to the months that consumed them; income deferred to the months that earned it. The largest lawful category, monthly by nature — Chapter 4 gives the procedures.

2. Payroll. The salary journal from the payroll register: debit salary expense (by cost centre), credit the net-pay liability (cleared by the payment run), credit the statutory accounts — PAYE, pension, other deductions — each a liability holding money withheld for someone else. Where the payroll module posts this automatically, read the generated entry against the posting map once anyway. Module 5 covers the Nigerian statutory detail.

3. Depreciation. Debit depreciation expense, credit accumulated depreciation — generated by the fixed-asset module where it runs (module 7), a governed monthly Journal Entry where it does not yet.

4. Bank charges and bank-side events. The charges the statement reveals: debit bank charges, credit the bank — entered as Bank Entries with the statement as the Reference, and only ever from the reconciliation (module 3), never from memory.

5. Opening balances. The go-live event: governed, evidenced, approved, loaded once. The critical rule: opening debtors and creditors load as per-party, per-invoice detail — through the Opening Invoice Creation Tool or per-document opening entries — never one total posted to a control account. The tie must be born intact. Module 4 details the migration procedure.

6. Owner and inter-entity movements. Capital introduced, drawings, director loans, movements between related entities — real events with no trading document. Journalised with the evidence referenced, parties where applicable, and the tax and legal shape decided by the accountant.

7. Corrections. Lawful only under Chapter 5's procedures.

The two tests. Whether a proposed journal belongs on this list:

1. The document test. Does a trading document exist for this event? If yes, the journal is forbidden regardless of convenience — the sale, the purchase, the stock move, and the payment all have documents.
2. The evidence test. Can the journal name its paper in the Reference fields — the agreement, the statement, the summary, the schedule? A journal that cannot reference evidence is an assertion, not an entry.

Practical rule: the lawful list for a given business fits on one page, and most of it recurs monthly. Chapter 7 turns that page into templates — after which anything outside the templates is, by construction, visible and reviewable.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Accruals and prepayments: the procedures
lessons.html:
The largest lawful category, with the exact procedures. The principle in one sentence first: the P&L should state what a month consumed, not what it happened to pay — payment dates are bank facts; expense dates are consumption facts. Without this, margins lurch with payment calendars and every monthly report reads noise.

Prepayment procedure. HealthTrade pays annual rent of ₦2,400,000 in January.

1. The payment posts to an asset: Payment Entry (or the rent invoice) debits Prepaid Rent ₦2,400,000, credits Bank. Eleven months of future occupancy is a thing the business owns.
2. The monthly consumption journal, twelve times: debit Rent Expense ₦200,000, credit Prepaid Rent ₦200,000.
3. Automate it: create the first consumption entry, then set up Auto Repeat on it (monthly, twelve occurrences) — or save it as a Journal Entry Template and post from the template each close. The User Remark is written once and rides every month.

Result: each month's P&L carries ₦200,000 of rent; the Prepaid Rent balance at any date is the occupancy still owed — a balance-sheet line that means something. The same shape serves insurance, licences, and subscriptions. (For deferred revenue and expense driven from items, the system can generate these schedules automatically — module 8's settings walk covers enabling it.)

Accrual procedure. The mirror. March consumes ₦180,000 of diesel and power; the bills arrive in April.

1. The close journal, dated in March: debit Utilities Expense ₦180,000, credit Accrued Expenses (a liability). March's P&L now tells March's truth.
2. The reversal: after submitting, use the Reverse Journal Entry action and date the reversal April 1st — the system builds the exact mirror and links the two.
3. April's actual bills post through their normal Purchase Invoices. The reversal has already cleared the estimate, so the actuals land clean — no double count.

The estimate → reverse → actual rhythm is the monthly craft. The close-checklist question that drives it: which consumptions have no bills yet?

The income side. Cash received ahead of earning is not income — it is a liability (unearned income) until earned, then a journal moves it to income as the earning happens. Deposits and retainers follow this shape; module 4 covers capturing customer advances properly at the Payment Entry.

Summary. Prepayment: pay into the asset, consume monthly by Auto Repeat or template. Accrual: estimate at close, Reverse Journal Entry dated the 1st, let the actual documents land. Income received early: liability first. Build all of it as templates; run it monthly, never annually.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Corrections
lessons.html:
Mistakes happen — the wrong account, the wrong amount, the wrong month. What separates clean books from reconstruction is how corrections are made. Four rules, with their procedures.

Rule 1 — history is never edited. A submitted entry is a permanent record. Corrections are new entries that reverse and restate, standing beside the mistake, telling the full story: error, discovery, repair. Even where permissions technically allow cancelling and amending a posted journal, prefer the visible correction — an edited past is a ledger that lies about its own history.

Rule 2 — reverse and repost, the procedure.

1. Open the wrong Journal Entry and use Reverse Journal Entry — the system creates the exact mirror, linked to the original.
2. Create the fresh entry with the correct accounts and amounts.
3. Cross-reference all three in their User Remarks: reversal of JV-0231, expense posted to wrong account; see JV-0233 for correct posting.

The GL then reads mistake — mirror — truth: three linked entries any reviewer reconstructs in a minute.

Rule 3 — documents are corrected as documents. The most-violated rule. When the error lives in a trading document — the invoice with the wrong customer, the receipt with the wrong quantity — the correction happens at the document:

• Cancel and Amend where the document chain allows it — the Cancel button, then Amend, producing the corrected document under a new revision.
• The returns and note machinery where trade has moved on — the Return / Credit Note button on the Sales Invoice, the Purchase Return on the receipt, the Debit Note on the bill. These correct the balance, the stock, the tax register, and the party ledger in one instrument.
• Never a Journal Entry patching the GL around the document. The patch fixes the balance while the document still tells the old story — and the party ledger, the stock ledger, and the tax register now all disagree with a GL that looks right.

The diagnostic that follows: a tie that will not reconcile almost always has a Journal Entry in it — and the fastest audit in this track is the General Ledger report on the control, stock, tax, and bank accounts filtered to Voucher Type = Journal Entry, where honest traffic is nearly zero.

Rule 4 — the period decides the date. An error found in an open month is corrected in that month, honest-dated. An error found after the close is corrected in the current month, with remarks naming the original period and entry — sealed months are not reopened for corrections (module 7 covers the close; module 8 the freeze settings).

Summary. Never edit; Reverse Journal Entry plus a fresh posting with cross-references; documents corrected by Cancel/Amend or the note machinery, never by journal; and corrections dated by the period rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The forbidden list and the system's fences
lessons.html:
Some journals are not merely governed — they are forbidden, because each one breaks machinery that cannot report its own breakage. The system fences some of them itself; the rest are policy. Learn each with what breaks.

1. Revenue journals replacing invoices. Debit Debtors, credit Sales, no Sales Invoice. Breaks: the VAT register (output tax untracked — a compliance failure), the customer's document trail (a balance with no invoice to allocate, dispute, or print on a statement), collections (nothing ages properly), and e-invoicing obligations where they apply. The purchase-side twin — expense journals replacing Purchase Invoices — breaks input VAT, WHT capture, and the supplier ledger the same way.

2. Journals to Stock-type accounts. The system's own fence: with perpetual inventory on, the form refuses Journal Entry rows against Stock accounts and raises an error naming the stock documents to use instead. The fence exists because a journal here moves the GL while the stock ledger stands still — the two diverge by exactly the journal's amount, permanently. If stock value is wrong, the error is in a stock document — a receipt's rate, a missing entry, a reconciliation — fix it there.

3. Journals to control accounts. Without a Party the form refuses the row. Even with a Party, treat control-account journals with suspicion: the events they usually claim — write-offs, discounts, settlements — have proper instruments (Credit/Debit Notes, Payment Entry deductions, module 4's provisioning) that carry the tax and ledger consequences the bare journal skips. Working rule: control-account journals are rare, party-carrying, and second-approved.

4. Journals to tax accounts outside the filing routine. Breaks: the register agreement — a VAT Payable that no longer equals what the invoice register says. Tax accounts move by documents and by the filing-and-remittance entries (module 5). The journal that forces the account to match a spreadsheet is backwards: reconcile the register, find the divergence, fix its document.

5. Journals to bank accounts outside real bank events. Breaks: the reconciliation — the GL bank balance acquires a row the statement will never show, an unexplained item forever. Bank accounts move by Payment Entries, Contra Entries, and the reconciliation's own charge entries — nothing else.

The shared shape. Every item on this list is the same mistake: a total adjusted around its details. The GL looks right; the machinery beneath disagrees; the disagreement surfaces later, further from its cause. When a standing agreement will not reconcile, run the Journal Entry filter on that account family first — it is the fastest diagnosis in this track.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Permissions, templates, and the monthly review
lessons.html:
Direct GL access is a dangerous power, and it gets the standard treatment: named holders, thresholds, templates, and a monthly review.

Who may journal. In Role Permissions, the Journal Entry doctype's create/submit rights go to the accountant and one named backstop — two people, not two departments. Warehouse operators, sales staff, and branch managers do not hold the pen; their corrections route through documents and requests. A journal can move any naira anywhere; the day everyone holds the pen, every fence in Chapter 6 becomes a suggestion.

Thresholds and second approval. Configure a submission Workflow on Journal Entry:

• Value thresholds route large journals to a second sign-off, even between the two named holders.
• Certain categories are second-approved regardless of value: anything touching control accounts, opening and closing entries, and corrections above the materiality line.
• The threshold numbers are the business's own policy, written down like every other control number.

Templates for the recurring set. Build the lawful monthly traffic once as Journal Entry Templates (and Auto Repeat where the amounts are fixed): accounts pre-wired, cost centres pre-set, remarks pre-written, amounts updated per period. Two payoffs:

1. The template list is the manual layer's honest census — a trading business's recurring journals fit on one page.
2. Everything outside the templates is, by construction, an event: visible and reviewable. The review question changes from are these thousand journals right? to the recurring set ran; what are these six others?

The monthly review, as a procedure.

1. Open the Journal Entry list; filter to the month; note the count (the standing health figure).
2. Read each entry against five questions: author, accounts, direction, date, story.
3. Bounce any storyless entry back for its User Remark.
4. Read the aggregate: the count trending up (the machine being declined), the same correction repeating (an upstream fault to fix at source), one author's entries clustering at period-end (a conversation).

Ten to twenty minutes at a healthy business, because the count is small.

Summary. Two named holders in Role Permissions; a Workflow carrying thresholds and category approvals; the recurring set as one page of templates with Auto Repeat; and the monthly five-question review, both per-entry and in aggregate.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's manual layer
lessons.html:
The month HealthTrade's manual layer was built, and the three tests that proved it.

The recurring set built (Chapters 3-4, 7). The accountant and the implementation team census the genuine journal traffic and build it in an afternoon:

• Rent: the ₦2.4m January payment into Prepaid Rent; the ₦200,000 monthly consumption entry created once and put on Auto Repeat, twelve occurrences, remark pre-written.
• Payroll: the salary journal template from the payroll register — expense by cost centre, net-pay liability, PAYE and pension custody accounts. Module 5's detail noted.
• Utilities accrual: the month-end estimate template. The estimate-reverse-actual rhythm is demonstrated live across March and April: March's ₦180,000 accrual submitted, Reverse Journal Entry dated April 1st, April's actual bills posting through Purchase Invoices, the net landing clean. The accountant, seeing the linked reversal work, builds two more accrual templates unprompted.
• Depreciation: a governed monthly template for now; the fixed-asset module noted for module 7.

The census closes at seven recurring templates — one page, as Chapter 7 promised.

A correction done right (Chapter 5). Week three: February's generator maintenance — ₦340,000 — is found posted to Repairs when policy wants it in Generator Running Costs, the line the MD reads separately. The temptation to cancel-and-amend the old journal quietly is declined out loud, as teaching. Instead: Reverse Journal Entry on the original (linked automatically), a fresh posting to the right account, and all three User Remarks cross-referencing. The drill-down from the MD's generator line now tells the whole story in four clicks. The accountant's comment: the books remember the mistake and the repair — that is what makes them believable.

A forbidden journal refused (Chapter 6). Week four: a branch manager calls — a customer disputes ₦86,000; just adjust the debtor and we'll sort it later. The refusal is the fence working: a journal to Debtors would move the control while no document tells the customer's ledger why; the printed statement would show a naked adjustment and the dispute would lose its paper trail. The routing instead: the dispute is investigated, resolves as a pricing error on one line, and a Credit Note is issued from the original invoice's Return button — correcting the balance, the VAT register, and the customer's statement in one instrument. The manager gets the outcome; the books get it the right way.

Month end (Chapter 7). The first monthly review runs from the filtered Journal Entry list: the seven templates fired on schedule, plus four others — each read against the five questions, one bounced back for an empty User Remark and resubmitted with its story. Review time: fourteen minutes. The count is noted as the layer's standing health figure.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the second law
lessons.html:
The manual layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the journal habit. Symptom: hundreds of Journal Entries monthly; sales and purchases journalised; the trading documents unused. Cause: manual-books fluency never transferred (Chapter 1). Fix: apply the document test to the whole traffic; migrate the biggest categories to their documents first — sales, then purchases, then payments; teach the transfer with respect; watch the monthly count as the recovery's measure.

Pattern 2 — suspense parking. Symptom: the balancing side nobody could find, parked in suspense; the account growing monthly. Cause: the one-sided instinct — posting what is known and warehousing the rest (Chapter 2). Fix: take the Difference field seriously (the other side always exists — find it or do not post), sweep suspense to zero monthly, and fix the classification gaps at source.

Pattern 3 — the tie-breaker journals. Symptom: control accounts disagreeing with their party reports; a stock agreement diverged by a suspiciously round number; a tax account matching a filing but not its register. Cause: the forbidden list violated (Chapter 6). Fix: the General Ledger report on the protected accounts filtered to Voucher Type = Journal Entry (the fastest audit in the track), each hit reversed and re-routed through its proper instrument, the fence re-taught, the pen narrowed.

Pattern 4 — the storyless journal. Symptom: entries whose User Remark is empty or says adjustment; reviews that stall on them; authors who cannot recall them. Cause: the remark rule unenforced (Chapter 2). Fix: require the story at entry, bounce storyless journals in the monthly review, and let templates carry pre-written remarks so routine traffic is never the problem.

Pattern 5 — the year-end journal storm. Symptom: a quiet ledger all year, then fifty journals in the close week — accruals never run monthly, corrections hoarded. Cause: the manual layer run annually instead of monthly (Chapters 4, 7) — every month's statements wrong all year, corrected once, when nobody remembers anything. Fix: the recurring set on Auto Repeat and templates, corrections posted when found, the monthly review keeping the layer current.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state what the Journal Entry bypasses and why the damage is silent; walk the form's fields and their rules (Entry Type, Posting Date, the Accounting Entries table, the Difference field, References, User Remark); recite the lawful list and apply the two tests; perform the prepayment procedure with Auto Repeat and the accrual procedure with Reverse Journal Entry; state the four correction rules and choose between Cancel/Amend, the note machinery, and reverse-and-repost; recite the forbidden list with what each breaks and which fences the system enforces itself; and run the monthly review from the filtered list with the five questions.

The second law: the journal is the exception and the document is the rule — what a document can do, a document must do. Module 3 takes the books to the bank: reconciliation.

banking.title: Accounts 3 — Banking & Reconciliation
banking.desc: Banking in ZhiftERP: the Bank-type ledger account, Bank Account record, and Mode of Payment mapping per real account; Bank Statement Import and matching in the Bank Reconciliation Tool with Create Voucher for bank-side items; the Bank Reconciliation Statement report; age limits for uncleared items; the imprest float and its invariant; the four-link cash-up chain recorded through Internal Transfers; and bank governance — prepare/release, masters-not-messages, mandate reviews, and the calendar.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Bank reconciliation: what it is and why monthly
lessons.html:
This module covers the banking layer of ZhiftERP: setting up bank accounts and payment modes, importing bank statements, the Bank Reconciliation Tool, handling the differences, cash and the imprest float, the retail cash-up chain, and bank governance.

The idea. The bank statement is a record the business does not write. Internal records can share one fault — the same wrong default poisons the invoice and the register together — but the statement states what money actually moved, when, and where. Reconciliation is the monthly comparison of the two records: every statement line matched to a ledger entry, every ledger bank entry matched to a statement line, and the unmatched remainder named and worked.

What reconciliation is not.

• Not a formality. A tick that examines nothing proves nothing.
• Not a plug. A balancing Journal Entry that forces agreement hides every real difference. Chapter 9 treats the plug as this module's most serious failure.
• Not optional at any size. The cost is about an hour per bank per month once the routine is established.

What an unreconciled business cannot know.

1. Whether its cash position is real. Decisions made on a GL bank balance the bank disagrees with are decisions made on a wrong number.
2. Whether payments landed — the transfer that failed silently, the cheque never presented.
3. What the bank has been taking — charges and deductions accumulating unbooked.
4. Whether anyone is helping themselves. The common frauds — the intercepted payment, the altered beneficiary, takings banked short — are caught first at reconciliation or not at all.

How ZhiftERP does it. The system's reconciliation is built from four parts, each with its chapter: the Bank Account record linked to a Bank-type ledger account (Chapter 2); the Bank Statement Import, which loads statement lines as Bank Transaction records (Chapter 3); the Bank Reconciliation Tool, which matches Bank Transactions against Payment Entries and Journal Entries (Chapter 3); and the Bank Reconciliation Statement report, which states the GL balance, the bank balance, and the explained difference between them (Chapter 4).

Module contents. Chapter 2: bank accounts and Modes of Payment. Chapter 3: importing the statement and matching. Chapter 4: working the differences. Chapter 5: cash accounts and the imprest float. Chapter 6: the cash-up chain from till to statement. Chapter 7: bank governance. Chapter 8: the HealthTrade case. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Bank accounts and Modes of Payment
lessons.html:
Reconciliation needs the setup right first. Three records per real bank account, walked in order.

1. The ledger account. On the Chart of Accounts, create one leaf per real bank account under Bank Accounts, with Account Type = Bank. Name it with the bank and account identity — GTB Current - 0123 — so every report reads plainly for years. Two rules follow:

• Never pool two real accounts into one leaf. Two statements cannot reconcile against one ledger.
• Never split one real account across leaves.

2. The Bank Account record. Open Accounting > Bank Account > New. Fill: Account Name, Bank (create the Bank record once per bank), Account Number, Is Company Account ticked, Company, and — the linkage that matters — the Account field pointed at the ledger leaf from step 1. The Bank Account record is what the statement import and the reconciliation tool work from; a leaf without its Bank Account record is invisible to both.

3. Modes of Payment. Open Accounting > Mode of Payment. Each mode — Cash, Transfer, POS, Cheque — carries an Accounts table mapping the mode, per company, to the ledger account the money truly lands in: Transfer to the receiving bank leaf, Cash to the cash account, POS to its settlement account. A mis-mapped mode makes every payment taken on it post to the wrong leaf: one bank's reconciliation fills with entries the statement will never show, and another's misses entries the statement does show. Verify the mapping at go-live by posting one test Payment Entry per mode and reading View > Accounting Ledger; re-check whenever a bank is added or changed.

Movements between your own accounts. Cash banked, funds moved between banks, the float topped up. Record these either as a Payment Entry with Payment Type = Internal Transfer (from-account and to-account on one document) or as a Journal Entry with Entry Type = Contra Entry. Nothing posts to income or expense. Both sides land on a reconcilable record: the sending side matches when the money leaves that statement, the receiving side when it arrives, and a transfer initiated Friday that lands Monday shows as an in-transit item both reconciliations can see. Chapter 4 sets the age limit on it.

Multiple banks. Businesses hold several accounts for real reasons — clearing, lending, payroll. Write each account's purpose in the Bank Account record's notes (operating, tax reserve, payroll), and review the list annually: every account should still have a job.

Summary. One typed leaf per real account; a Bank Account record linking each leaf to its bank and number; every Mode of Payment mapped and test-verified; internal movements by Internal Transfer or Contra Entry; purposes written down.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Importing the statement and matching
lessons.html:
The monthly reconciliation in ZhiftERP is two steps: load the statement, then match it. Run it per bank account, from the statement's own cutoff date.

Step 1 — load the statement. Open Bank Statement Import (search it from the top bar). Select the Bank Account, upload the bank's file (CSV or XLSX export from the bank portal), and map the columns — date, description, deposit, withdrawal, reference — the first time; the mapping is remembered. On import, each statement line becomes a Bank Transaction record with status Unreconciled. If a bank offers no clean export, lines can be entered as Bank Transactions manually, but push for the export: typing a statement re-introduces the typing errors the import exists to avoid.

Step 2 — match in the Bank Reconciliation Tool. Open Accounting > Bank Reconciliation Tool. Select the Bank Account and the period; the screen shows the closing balance per the bank and per the books, and lists the unreconciled Bank Transactions. Work each transaction with its action buttons:

• Match Against Voucher — the normal case: the tool proposes Payment Entries and Journal Entries with matching amounts; confirm the right one. Matching sets the voucher's clearance date, which is what marks a ledger entry as seen by the bank.
• One statement line covering several vouchers (a batched deposit), or one voucher split across lines: select multiple documents in the match dialog until the amounts agree.
• Create Voucher — for statement lines with no ledger entry yet: bank charges, interest, direct debits. The tool creates the Payment Entry or Journal Entry from the transaction, with the statement line as its reference. This is the only lawful source for booking bank-side items — never book charges from memory.
• A transaction that matches nothing and should not create anything — the bank's own error — is left unreconciled and queried with the bank until reversed.

Matching order. Run easiest to hardest: exact amount-and-date pairs first (the bulk), then amount matches with date drift (the payment entered Tuesday, on the statement Thursday — match it; the clearance date records the lag), then the composites, and last the remainder that will not match — which is not a failure but the month's worklist, handled in Chapter 4.

The proof. After matching, open the Bank Reconciliation Statement report for the account and date: it shows the GL balance, adds cheques and payments not yet cleared, and arrives at the bank balance. When that report closes with every listed item named and expected, the account is reconciled. When it closes only through an unexplained difference, it is not.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Working the differences
lessons.html:
Matching leaves a remainder on both sides. Each item belongs to one of three categories, and each category has a procedure.

Category 1 — timing items (book side). Entries in the ledger the bank has not yet seen: the cheque issued and unpresented, the transfer in transit, the deposit lodged after cutoff. These appear on the Bank Reconciliation Statement as uncleared items and normally clear next month. The discipline is a written age limit per instrument:

• Cheques — the validity window. A cheque unpresented at six months is stale; resolve it: contact the payee, and if the cheque is lost, reverse the Payment Entry by module 2's correction rules and reissue properly.
• Transfers — days, not months. In transit beyond a week means missing: trace it with the bank and find or force the reversal.
• Deposits — a lodged deposit missing from the statement is escalated the same day. Chapter 6's chain shows who carried it.

Read the uncleared list monthly with its ages. A remainder list that only grows is Chapter 9's Pattern 3 starting.

Category 2 — bank-side items, unbooked. Lines on the statement with no ledger entry: charges, interest, direct debits, standing orders, reversals, a customer paying straight into the account. Book each from the Bank Reconciliation Tool's Create Voucher button, statement line referenced. Two rules ride along:

1. Read charges before booking them. Compare against the bank's agreed schedule quarterly. Banks make errors, and a business that books blindly pays for them. Query and recover duplicates.
2. An unexplained credit is not income. Park it against a holding account, investigate the payer — it is usually a customer paying without a reference — and allocate it through the receivables tools (module 4) so the customer's ledger stays correct.

Category 3 — errors. Book-side errors surface here constantly: the transposed amount, the payment posted to the wrong bank leaf, the double entry. Correct each by module 2's rules — Reverse Journal Entry or cancel/amend the Payment Entry, with references and remarks. Bank-side errors are queried with the bank and tracked until reversed; never absorb them.

The monthly output. Finish every reconciliation with two artifacts filed: the Bank Reconciliation Statement report (printed or saved to the close bundle) and the aged uncleared list with an owner per item. The list's length and age are the reconciliation's quality measures.

Summary. Timing items ride under written age limits — cheque by validity, transfer by the week, missing deposit same day. Bank-side items book only through Create Voucher with the statement referenced. Errors correct by the rules. File the statement report and the aged list every month.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Cash accounts and the imprest float
lessons.html:
The statement covers electronic money. Physical cash has no outside record at all, so its rules are stricter.

Cash accounts: few and owned. Create a Cash-type leaf for each real cash custody — the main cash account, each petty cash float. Do not run one shared Cash account that several drawers post to: when several people share one balance, no variance can be attributed to anyone. Each custody gets a named holder, a counting schedule, and a written purpose. Design for minimisation: Nigeria's transfer-heavy payments make it practical to keep drawers few, floats small, and banking fast.

The imprest float, set up once.

1. Create the float's Cash-type account, e.g. Petty Cash - Head Office, and fund it to a fixed amount — say ₦100,000 — by an Internal Transfer from the bank.
2. Name the custodian. Disbursements happen only against a voucher: what, why, who, receipt attached. The vouchers accumulate in the box; nothing posts yet.
3. Replenish monthly: one Journal Entry (Entry Type: Cash Entry) debits each voucher's expense account with its Cost Center, credits the bank for the vouchers' exact total — restoring the float to ₦100,000. Attach the voucher scans to the entry.

The invariant that makes the float self-checking: cash in the box plus vouchers in the box equals ₦100,000 at every moment. A spot count takes two minutes and either ties or tells.

The cash count. Scheduled counts (the float monthly; tills daily — Chapter 6) plus unscheduled spot counts, because unpredictability is what keeps a counting programme honest. Count against the invariant, preferably by someone other than the custodian. Variance rules are the standard set: named the same day, investigated before adjusted, reason-coded, and tracked as a rate per custody. Frame the counts correctly with the team: the count protects the honest holder — a clean-count record is the custodian's own evidence.

Cash rules, itemised.

• Disbursements only against vouchers. No IOUs in the box — an IOU is an unauthorised loan on a scrap of paper.
• The float is fixed. Topping up by feel breaks the invariant.
• A spending cap routes anything substantial to a proper Payment Entry, where it gets approval and evidence.
• Custodian changes are a counted handover: outgoing count, incoming count, both signed, same day.

Summary. One Cash-type account per custody with a named holder; the imprest cycle — fixed float, vouchers, exact replenishment by one Cash Entry with cost centres; scheduled plus spot counts against the invariant; and the four cash rules.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The cash-up chain: till to statement
lessons.html:
Retail cash runs through a four-link chain from the till drawer to the bank statement. Each link produces a number, the numbers must agree, and each link has a named custodian. The till mechanics themselves belong to the ZhiftPOS track; this chapter is the accounts view of the chain.

Link 1 — the till session. Each till, each day or shift, is one session: opened with a counted float, traded through the till (every sale a document), closed with a counted drawer. One till, one operator, one session — a pooled drawer shared by several operators turns every variance into an argument, so it is refused.

Link 2 — the cash-up. At session close:

1. Count the drawer by denomination on a count sheet. "Roughly ₦180k" is not a count.
2. Compare against the session's system totals by mode: cash sales against cash in the drawer less the float; POS-terminal sales against the terminal's settlement report; transfers against the transfer log.
3. Name any variance the same day. A ₦14,000 short investigated at close is usually a training catch; found a week later it is an argument; a month later, a write-off.

Track cash-up variances as a rate per till and per operator. Rotating operators across tills separates the till from the person when a pattern appears; a clean-session streak is the operator's own record.

Link 3 — banking the takings.

• Intact: the whole count is banked — never the count minus informal spendings. Spendings out of the drawer break the tie between till total and deposit slip and skip all documentation; route them through the float or a Payment Entry instead.
• Fast: daily or next morning per policy; the overnight safe holds the minimum.
• The deposit is carried by a named person, and the deposit slip must equal the cash-up's banked figure to the naira. Record the banking as an Internal Transfer from the cash account to the bank account.

Link 4 — the statement. The deposit appears on the imported statement and is matched in the Bank Reconciliation Tool (Chapter 3). The full chain — till total → cash-up sheet → deposit slip → statement line — is one sequence of agreeing numbers. A break names its own link: till-to-cash-up is a session problem; cash-up-to-slip happened in counting or carriage; slip-to-statement is Chapter 4's same-day deposit alarm.

Summary. One operator per session; denominated counts compared by mode with same-day variances; takings banked intact and fast by named carriage, recorded as Internal Transfers; the statement match closing the loop monthly.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Bank governance
lessons.html:
Bank money moves at transfer speed, so its controls are the strictest in the system. Four sets, each a procedure.

1. Prepare and release, separated. The person who assembles a payment run (from approved invoices and matched documents in the system) is never the person who authorises it at the bank. Two people, at any size: at eleven staff, the founder releases what the accountant prepares. The run pays what the ledger supports — never what a message asks.

2. Masters, not messages. Payments go to the bank details stored in the Supplier record — never to details supplied in an email or chat. Changes to a supplier's bank details are a governed master-data event: verified through a known channel back to a known person at the supplier — never the phone number given in the requesting message. The urgent email from the "MD", the lookalike supplier domain, the convincing WhatsApp — each one dies against the process, which is the purpose of having one. The accounts team is this fraud's chosen target; refresh the training yearly and treat reported near-misses as wins.

3. Mandates and users. The bank-side mirror of system permissions:

• The bank mandate — who signs, at what thresholds, in what combinations — is kept aligned with the internal release design. Broader than the internal control is a back door; narrower is a bottleneck.
• Review the mandate annually and at every personnel change. A departed signatory is removed the week they leave.
• Online banking gets the same list: users named, limits set, tokens held personally, admin rights held by two named people.

4. The bank calendar.

• Monthly: reconciliation per account, with a written maximum unreconciled age — an account two months unreconciled is treated as an incident, not a backlog. The aged uncleared list read.
• Quarterly: the bank-charges read against the agreed schedule.
• Annually and on change: the mandate and online-user review.
• Per schedule: the cash counts (Chapter 5) and till sessions (Chapter 6).
• Daily, where cash is tight: the cash position across accounts. The Bank Account dashboard and the General Ledger report by account serve this read.

Summary. Preparer never releases; beneficiaries paid from the Supplier record with verified changes; mandates aligned, reviewed, and purged the week people leave; the calendar — monthly reconciliation with a maximum age, quarterly charges read, annual mandate walk.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's banking year
lessons.html:
HealthTrade's banking layer, installed and run. Every chapter appears.

Setup and the first reconciliation (Chapters 2-4). Three banks become three Bank-type leaves, each with its Bank Account record and written purpose — operating, tax reserve, payroll. The Mode of Payment mappings are test-verified (module 1's check had already caught one). Then the first reconciliation of the operating account, facing eighteen months of never-reconciled history. The statement files are imported month by month through Bank Statement Import, matched in the Bank Reconciliation Tool, and the remainder — 34 items — is worked by category:

• A nine-month-old stale cheque: ₦210,000 to a supplier who never presented it. The payee is contacted (the cheque was lost), the Payment Entry reversed with references, the payment reissued through the run.
• Fourteen months of unbooked charges, booked in one sitting through Create Voucher with each statement line referenced. The quarterly charges read then finds two duplicate charges; the bank refunds ₦38,000.
• One mis-mapped POS week — settlements posted to the wrong bank leaf during a terminal change. Corrected by the rules; the Mode of Payment mapping fixed.
• An unexplained credit of ₦127,000 — parked, traced within the week to a customer who paid without a reference, allocated through Payment Reconciliation (module 4) so the customer's ledger stayed correct.

Month two's reconciliation takes fifty minutes; month three's, forty.

The float (Chapter 5). The office drawer becomes a ₦100,000 imprest float: Cash-type account, named custodian, voucher pad, monthly replenishment by one Cash Entry with cost centres, voucher scans attached. The first unscheduled spot count in week three ties to the naira — cash plus vouchers equals one hundred — and the custodian asks when the next one is. Unscheduled, is the answer.

The cash-up chain (Chapter 6). Till sessions start at the retail counter. Day nine, the evening count is ₦14,000 short against cash sales — named that night, investigated while memory serves, resolved as two transfer-paid sales rung as cash by a new operator. A mode error, not a theft: the sessions corrected by document, the operator trained, the variance rate back at zero. Takings bank intact next morning by named carriage as Internal Transfers; slips match cash-ups; the statement matches the slips.

Governance (Chapter 7). The mandate review finds a former manager still a signatory eight months after leaving — removed the same week, and the trigger added to the leaver checklist. Prepare/release is confirmed live: the accountant prepares, the MD releases. By year-end the three banks reconcile in under two hours a month total, and the MD's note: the books and the bank now settle their differences monthly, and I read the result.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the third law
lessons.html:
The banking layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the never-reconciled account. Symptom: a GL bank balance nobody would rely on; decisions made on it anyway; the statement opened only to check if one payment landed. Cause: the comparison never performed (Chapters 1, 3). Fix: the first-dig reconciliation — it faces the whole backlog once; import the history through Bank Statement Import and work it — then the monthly routine, with the written maximum unreconciled age making relapse an incident.

Pattern 2 — reconciliation by plug. Symptom: accounts that "reconcile" perfectly every month via a balancing Journal Entry to a differences or suspense account. Cause: forcing agreement converts every real difference — error, fraud, drift — into a booked fiction; the account looks reconciled precisely because it never is. This is the module's most serious failure. Fix: excavate the plug account's history (each plugged amount is an unworked difference), forbid the plug, and install the name-every-item rule. An unexplained difference carried openly on the Bank Reconciliation Statement is honest; one booked away is not.

Pattern 3 — the museum remainder. Symptom: uncleared items riding for a year; stale cheques never resolved; in-transit items months old. Cause: no age limits (Chapter 4). Fix: the limits written per instrument, the monthly aged read with investigation at the limit, and the list's length and age on the close checklist.

Pattern 4 — cash counted never. Symptom: a drawer nobody can explain; IOUs in the float; petty cash topped up by feel; variances found annually and absorbed. Cause: the no-record asset given no rules either (Chapter 5). Fix: the imprest installed — the invariant makes counting trivial — custodies named and minimal, the count schedule with spot checks, the spending cap routing real expenses to Payment Entries.

Pattern 5 — the leaking chain. Symptom: till totals, cash-up sheets, deposit slips and statement lines each showing a slightly different number; takings banked late and light. Cause: the chain's links unsigned (Chapter 6) — pooled tills, undenominated counts, informal spendings en route, unnamed carriage. Fix: one operator per session, same-day denominated cash-ups, intact and fast banking recorded as Internal Transfers, and the four-link match run at every reconciliation.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: set up the three records per bank (typed leaf, Bank Account record, Mode of Payment mapping) and verify the mapping; run Bank Statement Import and match in the Bank Reconciliation Tool, including Create Voucher for bank-side items; read the Bank Reconciliation Statement report; state the three remainder categories with their age limits; set up and replenish an imprest float and state its invariant; walk the four links of the cash-up chain and what each break means; and state the governance set — prepare/release, masters-not-messages, mandate reviews, and the calendar.

The third law: every bank account is reconciled monthly, and every difference is named — never plugged. Module 4 covers receivables and payables from the accounts side.

ar_ap_chair.title: Accounts 4 — Receivables & Payables from the Accounts Chair
ar_ap_chair.desc: Receivables and payables from the accounts side: the monthly tie check against the Accounts Receivable and Payable reports; clearing floating items in Payment Reconciliation; advances captured against orders and consumed through the invoice's Advances section under the never-net rule; provisioning by aging matrix with the two-signature write-off workflow and recoveries; Process Statement Of Accounts and the supplier-statement mirror; per-invoice openings with the Opening Invoice Creation Tool; and the seven-step month-end routine.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The AR/AP layer and the tie check
lessons.html:
This module covers running receivables and payables from the accounts side: the reports, the Payment Reconciliation tool, advances, provisioning and write-offs, customer statements, opening balances, and the month-end routine.

The division of work. The sales desk chases customers; the purchasing desk pays suppliers. The accounts side owns the record: that the Debtors and Creditors figures are real, correctly aged, honestly valued, and complete. A receivable has no shelf to count — its entire existence is the party's ledger, the documents behind it, and the agreement between the control account and its parties.

The four questions. Read the receivables balance as four claims to verify:

1. Real — every naira attached to a Party and backed by documents.
2. Collectable — the provision question: ₦18.4m gross of which ₦1.2m is doubtful is a different figure.
3. Current — the aging honest, advances not netted against debts (Chapter 3).
4. Complete — nothing deleted, nothing parked off the ledger.

An external audit's receivables work is these four questions asked systematically. Keep them answered all year and the audit is short.

The tie check, as a procedure. Module 1 introduced it; this module runs it monthly, first, always:

1. Run the Trial Balance; note the Debtors closing balance.
2. Run the Accounts Receivable report as at the same date; note its grand total.
3. They must agree to the kobo. Repeat for Creditors against Accounts Payable.
4. On a difference: run the General Ledger report on the control account filtered to Voucher Type = Journal Entry. The cause is almost always there. Correct it by module 2's rules and never carry a divergence forward unexplained.

The two reports, introduced. Accounts Receivable (Accounting > Accounts Receivable): every customer's open items in aging buckets, based on due date — the collections worklist and the aging evidence. Accounts Payable mirrors it for suppliers. Both accept Party, Cost Center, and ageing-basis filters; the Summary versions give one row per party. These two reports, plus the Payment Reconciliation tool in Chapter 2, carry most of this module's work.

Module contents. Chapter 2: allocation and the Payment Reconciliation tool. Chapter 3: advances, both directions. Chapter 4: provisioning and write-offs. Chapter 5: statements and confirmations. Chapter 6: opening balances. Chapter 7: the month-end routine. Chapter 8: the HealthTrade case. Chapter 9: review and the law.
