lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Allocation and the Payment Reconciliation tool
lessons.html:
A party's ledger is entries; a party's readable story is entries matched — this payment against these invoices, this credit note applied to that invoice. Every unmatched item is ambiguity, and this chapter is the tool and routine that clear it.

What unallocated items do.

• A payment on account (received with no invoice references): the invoices it should have cleared still age as overdue in the Accounts Receivable report, while the customer's net balance looks fine. The aging now overstates, and collections may chase paid debts.
• A credit note issued but never applied: the customer's statement shows a debt and a floating credit side by side; the customer pays the net and disputes the rest.
• An advance never matched to its later invoice — Chapter 3's subject.

The balance can be right while the story is unreadable, and unreadable stories cost collections calls, statement disputes, and eventually the relationship.

The Payment Reconciliation tool. Open Accounting > Payment Reconciliation. Select the Company, the Party Type and Party, and the receivable/payable account. The screen loads two lists: unallocated payments and credit notes on one side, open invoices on the other. Select the items to match, adjust the allocation amounts where one payment covers several invoices, and click Reconcile. The tool writes the allocation — the invoices close, the payment stops floating, the aging corrects — without any new GL posting, because it is matching existing entries, not creating new ones.

The monthly unallocated read, as a procedure.

1. Run Accounts Receivable and filter or scan for negative and unallocated rows; do the same on the payables side.
2. For each party with floating items, open Payment Reconciliation and match. Where the customer's intent is unknown, ask them: your payment of the 14th — against which invoices? A normal, professional question, which also signals that the account is watched.
3. Genuine overpayments are refunded by a proper Payment Entry (Pay, referencing the credit), not left to confuse the aging.
4. Items nobody can explain after honest work are escalated by name — rare, and exactly what this routine exists to surface.

Why near-zero matters. Kept near zero: every statement is self-explanatory, every aging line is a real debt, and the monthly tie check is trivial. Lapsed for two quarters: the aging overstates, collections chase paid debts, statements teach customers to dispute, and the cleanup becomes a project. Grade each month's allocation discipline by this list's length — it costs one glance.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Advances, both directions
lessons.html:
Money moves ahead of documents in both directions: customers pay before invoices exist, and the business pays suppliers before bills arrive. Each direction has its handling.

Customer advances — a liability. Cash received ahead of earning is not income and not a negative receivable left to distort the aging. It is a liability: the business owes goods, services, or the money back.

1. Capture it as an advance. On the Payment Entry, when there is no invoice to reference, the amount stays unallocated — and where the order exists, receive the payment against the Sales Order so it is recorded as an advance on that order. The system posts the advance to the configured liability treatment rather than letting it float as a mystery credit.
2. Match it when the invoice books. The Sales Invoice's Advances section pulls the advance in (Get Advances Received), consuming the advance and settling the invoice in one step. An advance left floating after its trade completed is Chapter 2's most expensive case: the customer shows a debt and a credit nobody joined — and pays neither attention.
3. Report it as what it is — the never-net rule below.

Supplier advances — an asset, and a known trap. The advance paid to a supplier is a prepayment asset: pay it against the Purchase Order (the order's Advance Paid field tracks it), and pull it into the Purchase Invoice's Advances section when the bill lands. The trap this defends against: the advance paid, the goods arriving, and the bill settled again in full because nobody matched — the double payment. Two rules:

1. Age the advances. Review supplier advances monthly against expected delivery dates. An advance aging past its delivery is either a late supplier (an expediting conversation) or a claim quietly going stale.
2. Check for open advances before settlement. The invoice-entry step pulls advances before the payment run sees the bill; make this a workflow habit and audit it.

The never-net rule. Do not report customer advances netted inside the receivables line. ₦19.6m owed to the business and ₦1.2m owed by it are two different figures — an asset and a liability, with different risks and different tax treatment — not "₦18.4m receivable". The statements show them separately, always. The test: can a banker see the real position from the face of the statement?

Summary. Customer advances: captured against the order, consumed through the invoice's Advances section, never left floating. Supplier advances: paid against the order, pulled into the bill, aged monthly, checked before every settlement. Both directions reported un-netted.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Provisioning and write-offs
lessons.html:
Some debts will not be collected, and the books must say so before the auditor asks. Two stages, each with its procedure.

Stage 1 — doubtful: the provision. When collection is uncertain — the customer silent past every escalation, disputing without engaging, visibly in distress — the response is a provision: an estimate of the loss, charged now, while the debt stays on the customer's ledger and collections keeps working it.

• The entry: a Journal Entry — debit Bad Debt Expense, credit Provision for Doubtful Debts (create this account as a leaf under receivables' group so it reports against gross receivables).
• The size: by a written aging matrix, not by mood. Percentages per aging bucket, built from the business's own collection history — for example nil to 60 days, 10% at 61-120, 30% at 121-180, 60% at 181-365, 100% past a year. The Accounts Receivable report's buckets feed the computation directly.
• Each period, the matrix is run against the fresh aging and one Journal Entry adjusts the provision to the required level — up as a charge, down as a release. Keep the matrix stable (changed annually, as an event): then a provision movement means collections actually changed, not that someone turned a dial. Specific cases override the matrix in both directions, documented: the large debt with specific bad news provided fully regardless of age; the aged debt on a performing payment plan relieved with a note.

Stage 2 — bad: the write-off. When collection has definitively failed — the customer wound up, vanished, or pursuit costs more than the claim per policy — the debt leaves the ledger:

1. Evidence assembled: the chase history and dossier.
2. Approval on the two-signature path — configure the write-off Journal Entry (or the invoice's write-off) behind a Workflow with value routing.
3. The entry posts against the provision (or straight to expense where unprovided), with the tax notes captured — deductibility has conditions the accountant owns.
4. The customer record is retained, never deleted: written off is not erased, and the history matters the day the customer returns asking for credit.

Recoveries. A written-off debt sometimes pays. Receive it as a normal Payment Entry referencing the story in its remarks; it lands as income — and it lands cleanly precisely because the customer record survived the write-off. Chapter 8 shows HealthTrade's own case.

Summary. Doubtful: provision by matrix Journal Entry, debt stays, collections continues. Bad: two-signature write-off with evidence and tax notes, record retained. Matrix stable, movements explained, recoveries through the normal payment machinery.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Statements and confirmations
lessons.html:
The party ledger faces the outside world through four routines.

1. The statement run — automated. The customer statement is the party ledger, printed. ZhiftERP automates the run with Process Statement Of Accounts (search it from the top bar): select the customers (or a customer group), the period, the format (with or without aging), and either print the PDFs or — the useful part — schedule the tool to email each customer their statement monthly, automatically. Set it up once at go-live. The run returns three things:

• Collections pressure — the statement is the chase's standing reminder.
• Free error-checking — customers audit their statements: the missed payment, the unapplied credit, the invoice they never received all come back as queries, each one a correction you did not have to find yourself.
• Dispute hygiene — disagreements handled on record: the disputed invoice flagged in the system, the resolution documented, and the correcting instrument (a Credit Note from the invoice's Return button, an allocation in Payment Reconciliation, or a firm restatement of the debt) issued as a document. Never side-agreements in someone's inbox — a side-agreement contradicts every statement printed after it.

2. The audit confirmation. The auditor selects customers, sends balance confirmations, and compares replies to the ledger. A business that runs this module meets it with the four questions pre-answered: balances party-attached and documented (real), provisions on the matrix (collectable), advances un-netted (current), nothing deleted (complete). One courtesy shortens it: warn the selected customers that confirmations are coming — an expected confirmation gets a reply.

3. The supplier statement reconciliation — the mirror. The payables side has its own external record: the supplier's statement of your account, reconciled against your ledger (the General Ledger report filtered to the supplier, or the Accounts Payable report). Match their lines to your entries and name the remainder. What it catches:

• Invoices they show that you never received — a liability found before it arrives as a surprise demand.
• Credit notes they issued that you never captured — money owed to you, unclaimed.
• Payments you made that they never applied — the allocation conversation, from the other side.

Run it monthly for the top suppliers, on rotation for the rest.

4. Dispute records. Keep every dispute inside the system: the flagged document, the correspondence attached, the resolving instrument linked. Six months later the story reads itself.

Summary. Statements by Process Statement Of Accounts on a monthly schedule; disputes resolved on record by document instruments; confirmations met pre-answered; supplier statements reconciled — top names monthly, the rest on rotation.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Opening balances and migration
lessons.html:
Every AR/AP ledger is born in a migration, and how it is loaded decides whether the tie check agrees from day one or never has.

The loading rule: detail, never totals. Opening receivables load per customer, per open invoice — each balance decomposed into its actual open invoices with their numbers, dates, amounts, and due dates from the old records. Three things depend on it:

1. The Accounts Receivable report's aging is true from day one — every balance ages from its real invoice date, not from go-live.
2. Every future payment has real invoices to allocate against — Chapter 2's routine is possible at all.
3. The tie is born intact — the control equals the sum of real party detail.

The alternative — one opening balance per customer, or one Journal Entry to the Debtors control — produces a blind aging (collections priorities scrambled for a year), payments on account forever, and a control with no details. The same rule mirrors to payables: per supplier, per open bill.

The tool. Use the Opening Invoice Creation Tool (search it from the top bar): choose Sales or Purchase, and enter one row per open invoice — party, invoice number, date, amount, due date. The tool generates opening invoices marked Is Opening = Yes, posting against the Temporary Opening account so year one fabricates no revenue or expense. For businesses with clean export files, prepare the rows in the tool's template and load in batches.

The identity rules riding along.

• True dates where possible. Where the system's opening pattern forces a posting-date compromise, preserve the due dates — the aging runs on them. The accountant's call, documented.
• Advances load as advances — unallocated payments and order-linked advances, never netted into balances. Chapter 3's rule applies from the first day.
• Disputed balances load flagged, with the dispute history summarised — migration does not launder a dispute.
• The opening provision loads too: the matrix applied to the opening aging, posted as the policy's opening position — the honesty built in at birth, not retrofitted at the first year-end.

The migration reconciliation. Before go-live is signed off:

1. The new system's Debtors and Creditors balances tie to the old system's (or the signed trial balance's) totals, to the kobo.
2. The new Accounts Receivable and Payable report totals tie to the old party listings.
3. Differences — there are always some — are worked to zero or documented as deliberate corrections: the old system's known errors fixed at migration, listed, and signed.

Practical note: the detailed load costs days where the total-per-party load costs hours. Price it honestly at planning — the cheap load's real price is a year of blind aging and a tie that never agreed.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The month-end AR/AP routine
lessons.html:
The module's routines, assembled into one monthly sitting. About ninety minutes at a healthy business, one owner, run in this order.

1. The tie check — first, always. Trial Balance Debtors against the Accounts Receivable report total; Creditors against Accounts Payable; to the kobo. Agreement: one line, initialed — two minutes. Difference: an incident — the Journal Entry filter on the control account finds the cause; correct by the rules; never carry it forward unexplained.

2. The unallocated sweep. Chapter 2's read: floating payments and unapplied credits per party, matched in Payment Reconciliation, refunds issued properly, the unexplainable escalated by name. Grade the month by the list's length.

3. The advance aging — both directions. Customer advances against their expected completions; supplier advances against expected deliveries (the Purchase Orders' Advance Paid figures). Items past plausibility resolved or escalated. Confirm the reporting stays un-netted.

4. The provision review. Run the matrix against the fresh Accounts Receivable aging; post the one adjusting Journal Entry with its one-line explanation; document any specific judgments. Write-off candidates are surfaced to the approval workflow — the routine nominates, the governance decides, never both in the same sitting.

5. The statement run. Confirm Process Statement Of Accounts fired on schedule; work the queries that came back from last month's statements; verify open disputes are on record with their instruments.

6. Supplier statement reconciliations. The month's tranche — top suppliers monthly, the rest on rotation. Missing bills chased, unclaimed credit notes captured.

7. Outputs to the close. Hand upward (module 7's checklist receives them): the aged AR and AP with the provision shown, the advance schedules, the tie confirmation, the write-off log, the unallocated residue. One page each, and each already true because the routine made it so.

The economics. Skipped for a quarter, every list doubles and the catch-up becomes a project. Kept, the year-end AR/AP work is a formality and the audit's receivables questions are pre-answered. Give the routine one owner and a fixed slot in the month — a routine with a name and a date happens; one without either is an intention.

Feedback to the desks. The routine's findings — the recurring unallocated causes, the deduction patterns — go back to the sales and purchasing desks as process fixes, so next month's lists are shorter. The desks do not attend the sitting; they receive its output.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's year in the AR/AP chair
lessons.html:
The module's routines, installed and run at HealthTrade. Every chapter appears.

The sweep instituted (Chapter 2). Month one's first unallocated read finds the expected backlog: ₦840,000 floating across 23 items — payments on account going back nine months, four credit notes issued and never applied, two advances whose trades completed unmatched. Three afternoons in Payment Reconciliation clear most of it; customers are called with the standard question — your payment of March 14th, against which invoices? — one genuine overpayment is refunded by a proper Payment Entry, and one escalation (a ₦60,000 payment no record explains) resolves in week three as a sister-company transfer mis-referenced. The read closes month two at ₦45,000 and month three near zero. The corrected aging then shows two genuinely overdue accounts the old net balances had hidden — handed straight to collections.

The provision built (Chapter 4). The matrix is built from two years of the business's own collection outcomes: nil to 60 days, 10% at 61-120, 30% at 121-180, 60% at 181-365, 100% past a year — written on the policy page and run against the opening aging. Opening provision: ₦410,000, posted with its explanation to the MD: this is what the aging says the book is worth; the number was always true — now it is booked. Monthly movements after that are small and explained, and Q3's release reads as the good news it is, because the matrix had not moved.

A write-off and a recovery (Chapter 4). Month five: a customer definitively gone — premises vacated, phones dead, dossier complete. ₦188,000 written off on the two-signature workflow, evidence attached, tax notes captured, the customer record retained. Month eleven: the customer's principal resurfaces, restarts smaller, and pays ₦120,000 against the old debt. The recovery is received as a normal Payment Entry, referenced end to end, and the customer's history reads whole: debt, chase, write-off, recovery, new terms — cash only. The accountant's remark: the record survived the write-off, so the recovery had somewhere to land.

Statements and the mirror (Chapter 5). Process Statement Of Accounts is scheduled in month one: every open-balance customer gets a monthly emailed statement with aging. The first returned queries fix two allocation gaps for free. The first supplier-statement reconciliation of the top five catches a missing bill — an invoice the supplier shows that never reached the books — and an unclaimed credit note from a returns batch: ₦74,000 recovered by asking.

The routine settles (Chapter 7). By month six the sitting runs at its promised ninety minutes: tie checked in two, the sweep short, advances aged, one matrix entry, statements confirmed fired, the mirror's tranche done, seven one-page outputs to the close. The MD's year note: the receivables number used to be an opinion. Now it is four answered questions.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the fourth law
lessons.html:
The AR/AP layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the diverged tie. Symptom: the Trial Balance control disagrees with the Accounts Receivable report; nobody knows since when; reports quote whichever number suits. Cause: the tie never checked — journals to controls, total-per-party migrations, deletions (Chapters 1, 6). Fix: the Journal Entry filter finds the causes; date the divergence by working backwards; correct by the rules; and the monthly check makes the next divergence a one-month problem instead of a three-year one.

Pattern 2 — the netting error. Symptom: receivables that shrink when advances arrive; statements customers dispute on sight; a balance-sheet figure nobody can decompose. Cause: customer advances crushed into the receivables line (Chapter 3). Fix: advances captured against orders and consumed through the invoice's Advances section; reporting un-netted; and the banker's-view test applied to the statements.

Pattern 3 — the perpetual gross. Symptom: receivables at face value for years; aged debts immortal; the write-off unknown as an instrument. Cause: no provision policy (Chapter 4). Fix: the matrix built from the business's own history, the opening provision posted with its explanation, and the write-off workflow configured and used.

Pattern 4 — the silent ledger. Symptom: statements never sent; confirmations dreaded; supplier statements filed unread; disputes living in inboxes. Cause: the record hiding from examination — always a symptom of the hygiene it would fail (Chapter 5). Fix: the hygiene first (Chapters 2-4), then the routines switched on in order — Process Statement Of Accounts, supplier reconciliations, then the confirmation posture.

Pattern 5 — the immortal advance. Symptom: supplier advances aging past every plausible delivery; the schedule nobody reviews; the advance paid twice. Cause: advances anchored to no expected date and no monthly read (Chapter 3). Fix: advances paid against Purchase Orders, the monthly aging in the routine, and the pull-advances-before-settlement habit audited.

Pattern 6 — the deleted debtor. Symptom: customers who vanish from the ledger with their balances; a record that cannot answer for its own past. Cause: deletion used where the write-off belonged — completeness broken. Fix: the write-off as the only exit for a debt, records retained always.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: run the tie check end to end including the Journal Entry filter; clear floating items in Payment Reconciliation and state the three resolutions; capture and consume advances in both directions through the order and the invoice's Advances section, and state the never-net rule; size a provision from the AR report's buckets and post the adjusting entry; run a write-off on the two-signature workflow and receive a recovery; schedule Process Statement Of Accounts and reconcile a supplier statement; load openings per-invoice with the Opening Invoice Creation Tool and prove the migration; and run the seven-step month-end routine.

The fourth law: the record is kept real, collectable, current and complete. Module 5 covers the tax accounts and Nigerian compliance.

tax_compliance.title: Accounts 5 — Tax Accounting & Nigerian Compliance
tax_compliance.desc: Tax in ZhiftERP: the Tax-type custody accounts and the custody rule; the Nigerian frame with the 2025 reform and NGE Portal e-invoicing; VAT through the Sales and Purchase Taxes and Charges Templates and Item Tax Templates, with the Sales/Purchase Register bridges; WHT through the Tax Withholding Category and the Payment Entry Deductions table, with the certificate chase; the payroll deduction accounts and the tie chain; the six-step filing routine with the zeroing check; the compliance calendar and the tax-reserve account; and the authority encounter types.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The tax accounts: custody money
lessons.html:
This module covers the tax layer of ZhiftERP: the tax accounts and templates, VAT on both sides, withholding tax in both directions, the payroll deduction accounts, the monthly filing routine, the compliance calendar and the tax reserve, and handling authority queries.

The custody idea. Most tax money in a trading business is money the business holds for someone else, not money it owes from its own pocket:

• The VAT charged on every Sales Invoice was collected from customers for the state.
• The WHT deducted from a supplier's payment is the supplier's tax, held in transit.
• PAYE is the employees' income tax, withheld at source.

This is visible in the postings: all three are credits to liability accounts — module 1's ₦7,500 VAT line. The working consequence runs through the whole module: custody money is not revenue, not cash flow, and not available. A business that spends its VAT balance as working capital is spending someone else's money, and remittance day becomes a monthly crisis. Chapter 7's reserve procedure is the fix.

The accounts to create. Each custody is a leaf with Account Type = Tax:

• VAT Payable — output custody — and Input VAT — the claimable asset that offsets it (Chapter 3).
• WHT Payable — custody when deducting from suppliers — and WHT Receivable — the mirror asset: the business's own tax prepaid through customers' deductions (Chapter 4).
• The payroll deduction accounts — PAYE Payable, Pension Payable, and the levy family (Chapter 5).
• Separately, the business's own tax — the Companies Income Tax provision — which is a cost, not custody. Keep the distinction: withheld-for-others is custody; owed-from-profits is the business's own expense.

One pattern, five appearances. Every custody follows the same cycle: an account, fed automatically by documents and templates, reconciled monthly to a register report, cleared by a remittance Payment Entry, and verified back at zero. Learn the cycle once in Chapter 6 and apply it to each tax.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Nigerian frame. Chapter 3: VAT — templates, item tax, and the register bridges. Chapter 4: WHT — the Tax Withholding Category and the certificate chase. Chapter 5: PAYE and the payroll accounts. Chapter 6: the six-step filing routine. Chapter 7: the calendar and the reserve. Chapter 8: authority queries and audits. Chapter 9: the HealthTrade case. Chapter 10: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Nigerian frame
lessons.html:
The system machinery is universal; the obligations are Nigerian. This chapter is the map. Current rates and thresholds are the accountant's living knowledge — this manual teaches which machinery serves each obligation, not the numbers.

The taxes that touch a trading business.

• VAT — the consumption tax on supplies, collected on sales and remitted monthly, federal. Configured through the tax templates (Chapter 3).
• WHT — withholding on specified payment types, in both directions. Configured through Tax Withholding Categories (Chapter 4).
• PAYE — employees' income tax, withheld monthly, remitted to the state of each employee's residence. This split is worth memorising early: VAT and Companies Income Tax run federal; PAYE runs to states. One business, several authorities, one calendar.
• Companies Income Tax (CIT) — the business's own annual tax on profits, provisioned through the year; the accountant's territory.
• The payroll statutory family — pension, housing, insurance, and training levies (Chapter 5), applicability confirmed by headcount and sector.

The 2025 reform — what changed in practice. The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 and its companion acts consolidated the statute book and restructured administration. Three working consequences:

1. The authority landscape was reorganised, with registrations and filing rails updated. The accountant confirms the business's current registrations against the new structure.
2. Thresholds and reliefs were reshaped — small-company regimes, rate structures, exemption bands. The accountant re-reads eligibility annually; the system's job is to be reconfigurable: template rates adjustable, item categories re-flaggable, without disturbing history.
3. Compliance moved further digital — e-filing as the norm, and e-invoicing advancing. In ZhiftERP, FIRS e-invoicing runs through the NGE Portal integration, which transmits invoices to the authority's rails. The consequence that matters for this module: the authority increasingly reconciles your filed returns against your transmitted invoices automatically. A business whose returns are prepared from the system's registers matches by construction; one that files from a parallel spreadsheet gets the mismatch letters.

The boundary. This module teaches the machinery: accounts, templates, registers, routines, evidence. Tax positions — what qualifies, what rate applies, what relief is claimable — belong to the accountant and the tax adviser. Chapter 8 shows the boundary at its most important moment: the audit.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — VAT: templates, item tax, and the bridges
lessons.html:
VAT setup and the monthly position, end to end.

Output side — the sales templates. Open Sales Taxes and Charges Template. The standard template carries one row: Type = On Net Total, Account Head = VAT Payable, Rate = the current VAT rate. Set it as default; every Sales Invoice picks it up and posts the VAT to the custody account automatically. The Sales Register report (Accounting > Sales Register) is the document-level mirror: every invoice with its net and its tax, the return's raw material.

Input side — the purchase templates. The Purchase Taxes and Charges Template mirrors it: Account Head = Input VAT, an asset. The claim's evidence is the supplier's proper invoice — and for this reason invoice quality is a money question: a ₦100 price with claimable input beats ₦99 without. The Purchase Register report mirrors the sales side.

Item-level rates — the mixed-supply setup. Some items do not carry the standard rate. Configure this at the item, once:

1. Create Item Tax Templates for the non-standard treatments — e.g. VAT Zero Rated (rate 0 against VAT Payable) and VAT Exempt.
2. On each affected Item record, add the Item Tax Template in the Tax section. From then on, every invoice line for that item applies its own rate over the document template.
3. The distinction matters: zero-rated supplies still appear in the return and preserve input claims on their costs; exempt supplies fall outside the charge, and input VAT attributable to them is generally not claimable — the apportionment is the accountant's computation, fed by registers that can tell the streams apart.

A pharmacy whose basic-medicine lines ride an exemption while its cosmetics shelf is standard-rated gets this right at the item master — after which every sale classifies itself. Get it wrong there and every return inherits the error.

The monthly position. Output charged minus allowable input equals the position: payable in a normal trading month (remit the net), or a carry-forward credit in a heavy-buying month (the credit offsets future output; carry-forward is the practical road).

The two bridges — the pre-filing check. Before any return is filed:

1. Sales Register tax total for the month = VAT Payable account movement for the month (General Ledger report, filtered to the account).
2. Purchase Register tax total = Input VAT account movement.

Both to the kobo. A divergence found now is a bookkeeping task; found after filing, it is an amended return. With the authority reconciling transmitted invoices automatically (Chapter 2), the bridges are not good practice — they are survival.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — WHT: the Tax Withholding Category, both directions
lessons.html:
Withholding tax runs in both directions, and each direction has its setup.

As agent — deducting from suppliers. The system automates this through the Tax Withholding Category doctype:

1. Create a category per deduction type the business meets — e.g. WHT Professional Services — with its rate, threshold, and the account: WHT Payable. The types and current rates come from the accountant's table.
2. On each affected Supplier record, set the Tax Withholding Category.
3. On the supplier's Purchase Invoice or Payment Entry, tick Apply Tax Withholding Amount (it defaults on once the supplier carries a category). The system computes the deduction and posts it: the ₦1,000,000 professional invoice settles as ₦950,000 to the supplier and ₦50,000 credited to WHT Payable — the supplier's tax, held.

The agent's two follow-through duties:

• Remit monthly by the calendar (Chapter 6's routine; the account zeroes after).
• Deliver certificates. The certificate is the supplier's evidence for their own tax credit; an agent who deducts and never delivers certificates injures every supplier it pays. The deduction detail — who, what, when, how much — comes from the General Ledger report on WHT Payable grouped by party, or the withholding detail report; one listing serves both the remittance schedule and the certificate run.

As sufferer — customers deducting from you. Corporate and government customers deduct WHT from their payments: the ₦1,000,000 receivable settles as ₦950,000 cash plus a ₦50,000 deduction. The deduction is not a discount or a mystery short-payment — it is the business's own income tax, prepaid. Record it in the receiving Payment Entry's Deductions table: one row, account = WHT Receivable, amount = the deduction — so the invoice settles in full and the asset builds transaction by transaction.

Two rules make the asset real:

1. Capture at allocation. Every short-payment identified as WHT is coded to the Deductions row then, not investigated months later.
2. Chase the certificates. Keep the standing worklist: deductions taken, certificates outstanding, per customer, aged — worked like any receivable. An uncertificated deduction is money in limbo: suffered but unprovable.

Where the asset goes. WHT suffered offsets the business's CIT at filing — the credit the accountant applies, evidenced by the certificates. A business that never chases certificates pays its own tax twice, quietly, every year. Chapter 9 prices this at HealthTrade.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — PAYE and the payroll deduction accounts
lessons.html:
The monthly payroll splits each employee's gross into destinations, and each destination is an account with an authority behind it. The payroll run itself belongs to the ZhiftHR/Payroll track; this chapter is the accounts view.

The accounts.

• PAYE Payable — the employees' income tax, withheld under the current bands and reliefs (the 2025 reform reshaped them; the accountant keeps the table, and the payroll configuration applies whatever the current structure is). Remitted monthly to the state of each employee's residence: a Lagos office with Ogun-resident staff files in both states, so the payroll register must split by state.
• Pension Payable — employee and employer portions, remitted to each employee's chosen fund administrator. Several PFAs, one schedule: the register splits by PFA. This is the tightest window in the family — remittance is pinned to days from paying salaries, not to the month's end.
• The levy accounts — housing fund, insurance trust, industrial training — where headcount and sector make them applicable; the accountant confirms.

Hold the distinction from Chapter 1: amounts withheld from the employee (PAYE, employee pension) are custody; amounts borne by the employer (employer pension share, the levies) are the business's own expense. The salary posting credits the custody accounts and debits expense for the employer-borne lines; where the payroll module generates the posting, read it once against this map.

The payroll tie — a monthly two-minute check.

1. The payroll register's column totals: gross, PAYE, pension by portion, net pay.
2. The salary posting's lines match those totals.
3. The custody accounts' movements (General Ledger report) match the posting.
4. After remittance, the custody accounts return to zero.

One chain. When it holds, every payroll question is answerable in minutes: the employee disputing a deduction (the register row and the payslip), the state querying a remittance (the schedule and the receipt), the auditor sampling a month (the chain walked).

The payslip. Every employee receives a monthly payslip — gross, deductions itemised, net. It is the employee's version of the WHT certificate and the business's first defence in any deduction dispute. Not optional, not annual.

The annual layer. Employer PAYE returns file in the new year's first month. Where the payroll register lived in the system all year, the return is an extract; where salaries lived in a spreadsheet with a monthly lump journal, it is a reconstruction project — Chapter 10's Pattern 5.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The filing routine and the zeroing check
lessons.html:
Every custody clears through the same monthly routine. Six steps, in order, per tax.

Step 1 — close the register. The month's document-level detail, cut off at the period: the Sales and Purchase Registers for VAT, the withholding detail for WHT, the payroll register for PAYE. The register is the return's evidence and the account's mirror.

Step 2 — reconcile register to account. The bridge (Chapter 3's procedure): register total against the account's movement in the General Ledger report, to the kobo. Work any divergence now — before filing it is a bookkeeping task; after filing it is an amended return, an authority conversation, or both.

Step 3 — prepare the return from the system. The return restates the ledger. Do not compute it in a parallel spreadsheet: two computations guarantee a divergence, and the filed number wins the argument with the authority while the booked number wins it with the auditor — one source, or two problems. The spreadsheet's only lawful job is formatting the register extract into the filing layout.

Step 4 — file by the date. The calendar's line (Chapter 7), owned by a named person.

Step 5 — remit. One Payment Entry (Pay) from the tax-reserve bank account against the custody account, with the filing reference in Reference No and the return attached.

Step 6 — verify the zero. After a clean cycle, each custody account returns to its explainable level: zero for fully remitted custodies, the stated carry-forward for VAT credit months. Check it in the Trial Balance or the account's General Ledger. A custody account that will not zero is telling one of four stories:

1. A register-account divergence — the bridge was skipped.
2. A remittance short or posted to the wrong account.
3. A prior month's residue compounding.
4. Custody spent — Chapter 1's disease, surfacing as arithmetic.

The zero check costs one glance and catches all four.

The evidence file. Each cycle files its bundle: the register extract, the bridge reconciliation, the return as filed, the filing acknowledgment, the remittance Payment Entry, the zero verification. One folder per tax per month — attach the documents to the remittance entry and mirror them in the folder. This is Chapter 8's audit posture built monthly as a by-product; its absence is why authority queries paralyse unprepared businesses — the answer exists, but assembling it takes a week, and a week's silence reads badly.

Practical rule: steps 2 and 6 — the bridge and the zero — are the two that keep the routine honest, and the two that businesses under pressure skip first. Do not skip them.

checks.why: Before filing it is a bookkeeping task; after filing it is an amended return, an authority conversation, or both.

opts: A divergence, with the filed number winning the authority argument and the booked number the internal one
checks.why: The return restates the ledger; it is not a second computation.

opts: Closing the register at the period cut-off
checks.why: The register is the return's evidence and the account's mirror.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The compliance calendar and the tax reserve
lessons.html:
The routine needs its dates and its money.

The calendar. Build it once, with the accountant confirming the statutory days. The monthly shape:

• VAT — return and remittance in the month's third week, for the prior month.
• WHT — remittance on its earlier track; state-collected streams on their own days.
• PAYE — to each relevant state by its mid-month day.
• Pension — within days of paying salaries; the tightest window, pinned to the wage payment.

The annual layer above it: CIT filing on the business's horizon months after year-end; employer PAYE returns in January; the levy cycles. Record every obligation with its authority, day, owner by name, and evidence-folder location — on the policy page, reviewed annually and at every legal change. Set system Notifications or recurring ToDos against the dates so no line depends on memory.

The tax reserve. Chapter 1 named the disease — custody spent. The fix is structural: segregate the custody in cash, not just in accounts.

1. Open a dedicated bank account — the tax reserve — with its Bank Account record and typed leaf (module 3), its purpose written on the record.
2. Sweep the custody cash into it on a rhythm, by Internal Transfer: the month's VAT position at close (or as it accrues), WHT when withheld, the payroll custodies at the payroll run.
3. The rule: the reserve is not working capital. Remittance day then becomes a transfer from a funded account, executed by the calendar — no scramble, no bridging loan, no conversation about which supplier waits so the state can be paid.

The honest answer to "we need that float". Businesses under cash strain resist the sweep. The answer is not soft: the custody money was never available, so the strain is real and must be solved with real tools — collections acceleration (module 4), stock discipline, supplier terms, or actual credit at actual credit prices. Penalties and interest on unremitted custody are the most expensive credit line in Nigeria, taken by default. Chapter 9 shows this exact conversation at HealthTrade and the alternative that worked.

Summary. One calendar, every obligation with an owner and a reminder; one reserve account, fed by scheduled Internal Transfers; remittances as funded transfers; and the penalty line watched to zero — it is the single clearest measure of whether this module is installed.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Authority queries and audits
lessons.html:
Sooner or later the authority asks questions. The preparation is a posture built monthly, not a scramble.

The posture in one sentence. Registers tied to accounts tied to documents, filed on time, evidenced in folders. When that chain exists, every authority question is an extraction exercise; when it does not, every question is a reconstruction project — and reconstruction under deadline is where businesses concede assessments they never owed. The posture is Chapter 6's evidence file compounding: twelve folders per tax per year, each self-contained.

The three encounter types.

• The desk review. The authority's routine reconciliation of your filings against their records — increasingly automated as the e-invoicing rails mature: they hold your transmitted invoices and compare them to your returns themselves. A business whose returns came from its registers matches by construction; the mismatch letters go to the parallel-spreadsheet filers.
• The query letter. Specific questions on specific periods. Answer on record: in writing, evidence attached, within the stated window, factually, answering what was asked — completely, and nothing more. The accountant reviews every reply before it goes.
• The field audit. The authority in the building. Preparation is the standing posture plus logistics: a room, and a liaison — one named person through whom every request flows, so the audit receives consistent, logged responses instead of hallway answers. The role division is exact: the system's job is to produce evidence — registers extracted, drill-downs demonstrated, folders handed over — while positions are argued by the accountant and the tax adviser, never improvised at the table.

The common findings, pre-empted. What trading-business tax audits actually find, each one a chapter of this module skipped:

1. Output VAT on invoices absent from returns — the bridge skipped (Chapter 3).
2. Input VAT claimed on defective supplier invoices — the evidence rule ignored (Chapter 3).
3. WHT deducted but remitted late or not at all — custody spent (Chapters 4, 7).
4. PAYE state splits improvised — the register that could not split (Chapter 5).
5. Payroll postings that tie to no register (Chapter 5).

A business that runs Chapters 3-7 has pre-empted the list, which is the purpose of running them.

Summary. Build the folders monthly; answer queries on record and inside the window; route field audits through one liaison; produce evidence and leave positions to the professionals. A clean posture turns the audit from a threat into an appointment.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Case study: HealthTrade's compliance year
lessons.html:
The tax layer, installed and run. Every chapter appears.

The setup and the first clean cycle (Chapters 1, 3, 6). The four custody accounts are confirmed and typed. The item masters are audited for tax categories — the pharmacy's exempt basic-medicine lines against its standard-rated cosmetics: 14 items re-categorised with Item Tax Templates, after which the Sales and Purchase Registers can tell the streams apart and the apportionment goes to the accountant with clean data. Then the first full monthly VAT routine: registers closed, both bridges tied to the kobo, the return prepared from the register extract, filed, remitted from the new reserve by Payment Entry, VAT Payable verified at zero. The accountant's note in the file: first month the return and the ledger were the same document.

The certificate chase (Chapter 4). The WHT Receivable history is rebuilt from allocation records: ₦1.34m of deductions suffered over two years — certificates held for only ₦610k. The chase is instituted as a standing worklist: outstanding certificates per customer, aged, worked like receivables — corporate finance teams contacted with the professional ask, the government customer escalated through its due process. Eight months later, certificates for a further ₦590k are recovered and handed to the accountant for the CIT credit — the business's own tax, un-paid-twice. The remaining ₦140k, deductions by two defunct customers, is written to the accountant's judgment with its file: even the loss is a documented decision.

The reserve's first test (Chapter 7). Month four, a heavy import quarter squeezes cash, and the old instinct surfaces in a management meeting: the VAT reserve has ₦2.1m sitting idle — borrow it for the Emzor payment, replace it by the 21st. The custody rule is restated — the most expensive credit line in Nigeria, taken by default — and the alternative is worked instead: module 4's routine accelerates two collections, and a slow stock line is released. The reserve stays whole; remittance day passes as a funded transfer. By Q3 the reserve sweep is the month's first standing Internal Transfer rather than its last argument.

The desk query (Chapter 8). Month nine brings the authority's automated mismatch letter — for the pre-system period, where a parallel spreadsheet had filed what the old records could not reproduce. The reply is built on record: the current months demonstrated folder by folder (register, bridge, return, remittance entry, zero check), the legacy divergence quantified and explained, the accountant leading the position. The query closes with a small legacy settlement and one sentence in the closing letter worth keeping: current periods reconcile to source.

lessons.title: Chapter 10 — Common mistakes & the fifth law
lessons.html:
The tax layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — custody spent. Symptom: remittance day as a recurring crisis; the VAT balance funded by scramble; penalties and interest as standing line items. Cause: the state's money used as float (Chapters 1, 7). Fix: the reserve account with its scheduled Internal Transfers, the cash-strain problem solved with real tools, and the custody rule taught until it holds.

Pattern 2 — the parallel computation. Symptom: returns prepared in spreadsheets beside the system; filed and booked numbers diverging; nobody able to say which is true. Cause: two sources (Chapter 6). Fix: the return from the register extract, the bridges as the pre-filing gate, and the spreadsheet demoted to a formatting tool.

Pattern 3 — the unreconciled registers. Symptom: register totals and account movements drifting apart unexamined; the desk review's mismatch letter arriving as a surprise. Cause: the bridges skipped (Chapters 3, 6) — while the authority's e-invoicing rails run their half of the comparison automatically. Fix: the bridge as a standing monthly line, divergences worked before filing, the zero check closing every cycle.

Pattern 4 — certificates uncollected. Symptom: years of WHT suffered with a certificate file that fits in an envelope; the CIT bill paid gross. Cause: the sufferer side run on resignation (Chapter 4). Fix: the deduction captured in the Payment Entry's Deductions table at allocation, the chase as a standing aged worklist, and the recovered certificates handed to the accountant with their evidence — the module's most reliably self-funding routine.

Pattern 5 — payroll beside the system. Symptom: salaries in a spreadsheet, one lump journal a month, PAYE computed elsewhere, state splits improvised, the annual return a reconstruction project. Cause: a register that can produce any slice replaced by one that produces none (Chapter 5). Fix: payroll into the system or rigorously bridged, the tie chain checked monthly, payslips standing, the annual return reduced to an extract.

Pattern 6 — penalties as a cost of doing business. Symptom: late-filing and late-remittance penalties absorbed without comment, month after month. Cause: no calendar, no owners, no reserve — the module absent. Fix: the calendar with named owners and reminders, the reserve funded, and the penalty line watched to zero.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: create the typed custody accounts and state the custody rule; configure the Sales and Purchase Taxes and Charges Templates and Item Tax Templates for a mixed-supply business; run both VAT bridges from the register reports to the General Ledger; set up a Tax Withholding Category on a supplier and record a customer's deduction in the Payment Entry Deductions table; state the payroll tie chain and the payslip rule; run the six-step routine and read the zero check's four stories; build the calendar and the reserve with its Internal Transfer sweeps; and state the three authority encounter types with the evidence posture.

The fifth law: tax money is held, not owned — reconciled to its registers, filed from the system, remitted from the reserve, and zeroed every cycle. Module 6 covers cost centres and dimensions.

dimensions.title: Accounts 6 — Cost Centers & Dimensions
dimensions.desc: Cost centres and dimensions in ZhiftERP: the Cost Center tree built from the accountability structure; defaults (Company, item, POS Profile), the cascade, and Mandatory For Profit and Loss validation with the unaddressed check; the branch P&L read as contribution before fully-loaded with the close-on-contribution rule; the allocation rules; the Budget doctype with Monthly Distribution, Stop/Warn actions, and the Budget Variance Report; and Accounting Dimensions with the three-part earning test plus the Project field for job costing.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Cost centres: one chart, many readings
lessons.html:
This module covers the address layer of ZhiftERP: the Cost Center tree, the defaults and validation that put an address on every posting, the branch profit read, allocating shared costs, budgets, and additional dimensions for service lines and projects.

The question it answers. Every owner of a multi-branch business asks it: which branch actually makes money? Without structure the answer is folklore — the flagship "carries" the network, the new branch "must be losing". The structured answer requires every naira of revenue and cost to carry, from the moment it posts, an address: the branch, line, or project it belongs to. In ZhiftERP that address is the Cost Center field, present on every posting row, and the P&L filtered by cost centre is the answer read directly.

The design rule: one chart, many readings. The Chart of Accounts answers what kind of money; cost centres answer whose and where. Rent is one account everywhere; Rent at Ibadan is the same account read through the Ibadan cost centre filter.

The mistake this prevents. The alternative seen constantly in the wild: per-branch account copies — Rent - Ibadan, Rent - Akure, Rent - HQ, repeated for every expense. Three branches turn a 60-line P&L into 180 accounts; five branches into 300; every new branch becomes chart surgery; every firm-wide read is assembled by hand; and the mis-post rate rises with the count of near-identical names. The test of a correct design: opening branch four should touch the cost centre list and not one account.

What cost centres are not.

• Not a second chart. A cost centre holds no balance of its own — it is a tag on GL rows, and every cost-centre read is the same General Ledger, filtered.
• Not free. Every mandatory dimension is a field the front line must fill (or defaults must fill for them) on every posting, forever. Chapter 7 guards the door on adding more.

Module contents. Chapter 2: building the Cost Center tree. Chapter 3: defaults, the cascade, and mandatory validation. Chapter 4: the branch P&L — contribution before fully-loaded. Chapter 5: allocating shared costs. Chapter 6: the Budget doctype and the variance read. Chapter 7: Accounting Dimensions — service lines and projects. Chapter 8: the HealthTrade case, from the design hour to the first budget cycle. Chapter 9: review, the recurring failure patterns, and the module's law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Building the Cost Center tree
lessons.html:
Open Accounting > Cost Center. Like the Chart of Accounts, it is a tree: group cost centres for rollup reading, leaf cost centres that take postings. Postings to groups are refused. The company's tree roots at its main cost centre.

Creating the tree. Use Add Child from the tree view: Cost Center Name, parent, Is Group for folders. The same tree rules as the chart apply: named plainly for the long term, shallow (two levels below root serves almost every trading business), and changed as governed events — a cost centre with history is disabled, not deleted.

What earns a leaf. The design question is whose performance the business manages — the accountability structure, not the org chart:

• A leaf per unit with an owner and a monthly profit conversation: each branch (a manager answers for it); Head Office (the shared-cost home Chapter 5 allocates from); a distribution or warehouse operation where it is managed as its own unit.
• Not a leaf per paper department, per two-person team, or per activity nobody reviews. A cost centre that nobody's monthly conversation names is clutter with a name.

A shortcut: the cost centre tree usually mirrors the warehouse tree's accountability layer — the people who answer for stock usually answer for the profit. Where the two trees differ, the difference should be explainable in one sentence.

Where the defaults live. Three layers carry the addressing work so the front line rarely touches the field:

1. The Company record's Default Cost Center — the fallback for unaddressed postings. Chapter 3's target is that this fallback almost never fires.
2. Master defaults: the Item record's defaults table carries a Selling and Buying Cost Center per company (useful where product-line reading matters); the POS Profile carries the branch's cost centre so every till sale lands addressed; recurring documents and templates carry theirs.
3. Document defaults: the Sales Invoice and Purchase Invoice carry a header-level Cost Center that flows to their rows.

The design goal: ninety-something percent of postings addressed without anyone touching the field, because the setup wrote the address. Defaults do not decay; discipline does.

Practical rule: keep the leaf count honest. Each leaf is a monthly page someone must own and read. A tree with more leaves than owners is telling you which ones to merge.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The cascade and mandatory validation
lessons.html:
An address book is useless if postings go unaddressed. This chapter is the wiring: where the Cost Center field appears, how defaults resolve, and the validation that makes the address a rule.

Where the field appears. Every P&L-touching document carries it at two levels:

• Header level — the whole document one address: the branch's Sales Invoice, the branch's expense claim.
• Row level — each line its own: the head-office purchase split across branches, the invoice mixing lines. The row overrides the header, because real documents mix addresses more often than designs expect.

The posting map (module 1) gains its address column: the Sales Invoice's income rows carry the selling branch (from the POS Profile, the header, or the item default); the Delivery Note's COGS rows carry the same; the Purchase Invoice's expense rows carry their consumers, row-level where consumption splits; Journal Entry rows carry theirs — module 2's form already requires it on expense rows; the salary posting carries each employee's unit.

The cascade. Defaults resolve specific-beats-general:

1. The row's explicit entry, over
2. The document header's Cost Center, over
3. The master default (item, POS Profile, template), over
4. The Company's Default Cost Center.

Set the masters so the front line almost never sees the field: the Ibadan till's sales land at Ibadan because the POS Profile says so; the Akure expense lands at Akure because the header does. The field surfaces for a human decision only where the machine cannot know — the shared purchase, the split service — which is exactly where a human should decide.

Mandatory validation. Two settings close the gap between mostly-addressed and always-addressed:

1. On each Account that must always carry an address, the cost centre can be made required; and system-wide, the Accounting Dimension framework (Chapter 7) carries per-company checkboxes — Mandatory For Profit and Loss Account and Mandatory For Balance Sheet — that refuse any posting to those account families without the dimension filled.
2. Turn on Mandatory For Profit and Loss at minimum. A P&L posting then cannot save blank, and the Company fallback catches only what validation deliberately exempts.

The monthly test. Run the General Ledger (or P&L) filtered to the Company's default cost centre: the unaddressed amount should be zero or near it. A growing figure means a cascade gap or a bad exemption — sweep it to true addresses while small, and fix the gap at its source.

Practical rule: verify the wiring like the posting map — one live document per kind, the addresses read aloud from View > Accounting Ledger. An hour at setup buys a P&L that filters true from month one.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The branch P&L: contribution before fully-loaded
lessons.html:
The addresses exist so this report can run: open the Profit and Loss Statement and filter by Cost Center — the branch's page, monthly. The read has two versions, and keeping them separate is the chapter's whole discipline.

The contribution view — facts only. Filtered to the branch, the P&L assembles from the wiring: the branch's revenue (every sale carried its source), the branch's COGS (the delivery rows carried it too), and the branch's direct expenses — its rent, payroll, power, local running costs, each posted with its address at entry. Contribution = branch revenue − branch COGS − branch direct costs. Every number on this page is a fact: posted where it happened, nothing estimated, nothing arguable. This is the branch manager's page — they control everything on it. Its honesty is exactly the wiring's honesty, and for this reason Chapter 3's unaddressed check precedes every monthly read.

The fully-loaded view — facts plus policy. Head Office exists — the MD's salary, the accountant, shared marketing, the system subscription — and none of it posts to a branch because none of it belongs to one. The fully-loaded view subtracts an allocated share of Head Office from each branch's contribution. Its numbers are part fact, part policy, because the allocation basis is a choice (Chapter 5). This is the owner's portfolio page — worth seeing, dangerous to act on alone. Show allocated lines as allocated: labelled, separable, never blended into direct costs.

The classic misread, with its arithmetic. The newest branch shows a fully-loaded loss — its allocated overhead share swamps its young contribution — and someone proposes closing it. Walk the numbers before agreeing:

1. Close the branch: its contribution leaves the network.
2. The allocated overhead does not leave — it re-lands on the surviving branches.
3. The business is poorer by the closed branch's contribution, and the loaded view now frowns at the next-smallest branch.

The rule that prevents the spiral: open, close, and expand on contribution; use the loaded view only to size the head-office conversation. Chapter 8 shows the rule at HealthTrade's Akure branch.

The monthly read, as a procedure.

1. Run the unaddressed check (Chapter 3).
2. Run the P&L per branch cost centre, contribution format, branches side by side.
3. Read trends against prior months; drill any surprise to its documents.
4. Produce the loaded view separately, labelled, for the owner's sitting.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Allocating shared costs
lessons.html:
Head Office's costs either stay unallocated — honest, but the loaded view stays unbuilt — or are shared by rule. The rules are short, written, and deliberately routine.

Rule 1 — direct first, always. Everything attributable at source posts there and never enters allocation: the marketing campaign run for one branch's opening posts to that branch; the head-office staffer seconded to a project posts to the project; the shared warehouse's costs, where it serves branches measurably, can be recharged by throughput. Every naira attributed directly is a naira the allocation argument never touches. Mature businesses allocate a residue, not a bloc — the smaller the allocated pool, the smaller the fiction and the quieter the arguments.

Rule 2 — a written basis per cost family. What remains shares by a basis recorded on the policy page:

• Revenue share — the default for general overheads: simple, proportional to activity.
• Headcount — for people-driven costs: HR, welfare, training.
• Space — for premises costs where premises are shared.
• Throughput — for the distribution recharge, where measured.

Three properties matter more than the specific numbers:

1. Written — every allocation question is answered by pointing at the page, not arguing.
2. Stable — changed annually at most, as an event with a memo. A basis that moves monthly is a dial, and then movements mean nothing.
3. Visible — allocated lines shown as allocated on the loaded view, labelled and separable, so any reader can reconstruct contribution by covering one section.

Posting mechanics. Keep it simple: the allocation is a reporting computation on the loaded view wherever possible. Where the business wants allocations in the ledger, post one monthly Journal Entry per basis — debit each branch's cost centre, credit Head Office's — from a saved template, and reverse-and-repost when the basis changes at year boundary. (The system also offers distributed cost-centre percentage splitting for automatic apportionment at posting time; introduce it only after the written basis has been stable for a year.)

The allocation wars, and the treaty. Where allocation is argued monthly, the same three failures are present: the basis is unwritten or unstable; the pool is too large because direct-first was neglected; and the loaded view is being used for decisions it cannot carry — branch bonuses on loaded profit is the classic accelerant. The treaty reverses all three: direct-first shrinks the pool, the written basis freezes annually, the lines stay labelled, and incentives move to contribution — the page the manager actually controls.

Practical rule: when an allocation argument starts, point at the page. If the page cannot settle it, fix the page once instead of having the argument monthly.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Budgets: the Budget doctype and the variance read
lessons.html:
Cost centres address the past; budgets address the future. The system joins them: the budget per address, the actuals landing beside it, and the monthly variance read.

The Budget doctype. Open Accounting > Budget > New:

• Budget Against — Cost Center (or Project). One Budget record per cost centre per fiscal year.
• Company / Fiscal Year — the containers.
• Monthly Distribution — optional link to a Monthly Distribution record carrying the seasonal curve: the even split for steady costs, the December-heavy curve for retail that expects its own Q4.
• The Accounts table — one row per account (or group) with its annual budget amount.
• Actions on exceeding — for annual and cumulative-monthly breaches, choose Stop, Warn, or Ignore, and whether the check applies on Material Request, Purchase Order, or actual posting. Reserve Stop for account families where overspend is a control failure; a Stop on COGS in a good sales month is the system fighting the trade. Warn widely, stop narrowly.

Building budgets that mean something. Budget quality is structural:

1. Built per address from that address's own history — last year's actuals per cost centre, which the system supplies by construction: the address layer's first forward payoff.
2. Adjusted by known changes — the new branch's ramp, the rent review, the headcount plan.
3. Owned by the address's owner — the branch manager who built their number defends it differently than one who received it.
4. Approved as a set — the rollup reconciles to the business's plan. Branch ambitions summing past the network's cash is a November conversation, not a March discovery.

The variance read. Run the Budget Variance Report monthly: actual against budget, by cost centre, by account, monthly and cumulative. One discipline: cause before comment. A material variance decomposes — volume versus rate (more units, or more per unit), timing versus level (a cost that moved months, or a cost that grew), one-off versus run-rate (the repair that happened, or the drift that will repeat) — and the read's output is the material variances, each with a one-line cause and, where needed, an action with an owner. Thresholds keep it short; the read exists for the stories, not the noise.

Practical rule: a budget cited in January and December and absent between is decoration; a budget used mainly for blame teaches managers to pad numbers and hide news. The monthly read, seated in the close, is what keeps the instrument alive.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Accounting Dimensions: service lines and projects
lessons.html:
The cost centre answers where. Some businesses need a second question answered — what line, which job — and the system carries it without touching the chart.

The Accounting Dimension doctype. Open Accounting > Accounting Dimension > New, choose the reference doctype (create a small doctype such as Service Line, or use an existing one), and the system adds that field to every accounting document and GL row automatically. Per company, the dimension carries two checkboxes — Mandatory For Profit and Loss Account and Mandatory For Balance Sheet — the same validation machinery Chapter 3 used for cost centres. Every financial report then offers the dimension as a filter.

When a second dimension earns its field. The test is strict, because every mandatory dimension taxes every posting forever. All three must hold:

1. Someone will read its cut monthly and act on it.
2. The cut crosses the cost centre — the service line that exists at several branches. A line that lives inside one branch is already carried by the cost centre tree.
3. It can be attributed at entry with reasonable defaults — a dimension the front line cannot fill truthfully will be filled falsely, and the layer's honesty is only ever the entry moment's honesty.

Two dimensions serve almost every trading business that needs any; a third is rare and argued hard; a fourth produces reads nobody trusts.

The service-line lens. The mixed business's standing need — the pharmacy with a clinic corner, the retailer with an installation arm: one branch, two businesses, and the branch P&L alone cannot say which earns. Set item-group or item defaults so invoice rows carry their line automatically (clinic services default to Clinic, shop items to Retail), post the line's direct costs with the same tag, and the pair of dimensions unlocks the branch-by-line matrix: Ibadan's clinic against Akure's clinic, each branch's retail core. That matrix answers expansion's real question — not should we add clinics, but the clinic contributes X at Ibadan and Y at Akure; what differs, and which model travels? Contribution framing governs exactly as in Chapter 4.

The project lens. Job-shaped work — the fit-out contract, the installation, the one-off tender — uses the built-in Project field: create the Project, tag its invoices, purchases, and timesheet-driven costs, and read revenue, cost, and margin per job in the project reports. Projects have what branches do not: a lifecycle — opened with a code and an owner, read at completion against the quote (the estimating feedback loop), and closed so the open list stays short. A project list full of ancient open codes is the dimension decaying into noise.

Practical rule: before creating any dimension, write down the monthly read it will serve and name its reader. No named reader, no dimension.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's addresses
lessons.html:
The address layer, installed and read. Every chapter appears.

The tree and the wiring (Chapters 2-3). The design hour with the MD and the accountant produces four leaves under two groups — Branches (Central/Lagos, Ibadan, Akure) and Head Office — mirroring the warehouse tree's accountability layer. The one difference gets its one-sentence justification: the shared distribution operation takes its own leaf because it is managed and read as a unit. The POS Profiles carry their branch cost centres; item defaults are set where line reading matters; Mandatory For Profit and Loss validation is switched on; and the posting map is re-verified with its address column — one live document per kind, the addresses read from View > Accounting Ledger. Month one's unaddressed check: ₦0 — the validation refused every blank at birth.

The first branch P&L, and the MD's lesson (Chapter 4). Month two, the P&L runs per branch, contribution format, three branches side by side: Central strong, Ibadan solid — and Akure, eight months old, contributing ₦310,000… which the fully-loaded view (Head Office allocated by revenue share) turns into a ₦140,000 "loss". The MD's first instinct is the classic — Akure isn't working — and the arithmetic is walked on the whiteboard: close Akure and its ₦310k contribution leaves the network; the allocated overhead stays and re-lands on Central and Ibadan; the business is ₦310k a month poorer, and the loaded view now frowns at Ibadan. The rule lands — close on contribution, expand on contribution — and Akure, read rightly, is a young branch working. The loaded view keeps its one real job: it sizes the head-office conversation, which produces one genuine action — the software and admin stack is renegotiated and Head Office lightens 8%, improving every branch's loaded view without a single allocation argument.

The policy settles an argument (Chapter 5). Month four, the Ibadan manager disputes the marketing allocation — a campaign that only helped Lagos. The policy page answers by pointing: branch-attributable campaigns post direct — and this one, on inspection, was indeed Lagos-specific, mis-posted to the shared pool and corrected to Central's direct costs by the rules. The residue keeps sharing by the written basis. The argument ends in one meeting because the page decides, not the loudest voice.

Budgets arrive (Chapter 6). Year two's Budget records are created per branch cost centre from each branch's own year-one actuals, adjusted for known changes (Akure's ramp, the Central rent review), owned by the managers who built them, approved as a reconciling set, with Warn actions on the expense families and a Monthly Distribution carrying the trade's seasonality. The Budget Variance Report seats itself in the monthly close — causes before comments — and February's first real story (Ibadan's power spend up 40%: a generator fault, one-off, fixed) is discussed in week one instead of surfacing in a year-end argument.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the sixth law
lessons.html:
The address layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the per-branch chart copy. Symptom: Rent-Ibadan, Rent-Akure, Rent-HQ… hundreds of accounts, chart surgery at every opening, firm-wide reads assembled by hand. Cause: the address written into the account names — cost centres unknown or distrusted at setup (Chapter 1). Fix: the migration — cost centres wired, the copies merged to single accounts by documented entries with history preserved, validation switched on, the chart returned to one language. Priced honestly: it is real work, done once.

Pattern 2 — the unaddressed lump. Symptom: the Company's default cost centre absorbing a growing share of the P&L; branch reads everyone quietly distrusts. Cause: the address optional in practice — blanks accumulating where validation should refuse them (Chapter 3). Fix: the lump swept to true addresses while small, Mandatory For Profit and Loss switched on, the master defaults tightened so the field rarely surfaces, and the monthly unaddressed check kept before every branch read.

Pattern 3 — allocation wars. Symptom: monthly arguments over shared-cost shares; bonuses fought over loaded profit; the basis renegotiated by whoever argues loudest. Cause: the rules absent (Chapter 5) — pool too large, basis unwritten, the loaded view carrying decisions it cannot. Fix: direct-first shrinking the pool, the written basis frozen annually, labelled lines, incentives moved to contribution.

Pattern 4 — the death-spiral close. Symptom: the smallest branch closed on its loaded loss; the network poorer; the next branch now "losing". Cause: allocation-led decisions (Chapter 4). Fix: the arithmetic taught before it is needed, contribution governing open/close/expand, the loaded view restricted to sizing the overhead conversation.

Pattern 5 — budget theatre. Symptom: budgets built in January, cited in December, absent between; managers padding numbers and hiding news. Cause: the instrument used as decoration or as punishment (Chapter 6) — either kills the conversation it exists to create. Fix: the Budget Variance Report seated in the monthly close, thresholds surfacing stories not noise, causes before comments.

Pattern 6 — dimension fog. Symptom: several mandatory dimensions; the front line inventing values to save documents; every read doubted. Cause: dimensions added without the three-part test (Chapter 7). Fix: the test applied retroactively — unread dimensions retired, entry honesty restored, and the rule going forward: no named reader, no dimension.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: build the Cost Center tree from the accountability structure and state the branch-four test; set the defaults (Company, item, POS Profile) and the cascade order, switch on Mandatory For Profit and Loss, and run the unaddressed check; produce the branch P&L in contribution format and walk the close-on-contribution arithmetic; state the allocation rules — direct first; written, stable, visible bases — and the treaty; create a Budget with Monthly Distribution and actions, and run the Budget Variance Report with cause-before-comment; and create an Accounting Dimension, state the three-part earning test, and use the Project field for job costing.

The sixth law: one chart, many readings — every posting carries its address, contribution decides, and allocation is written. Module 7 assembles the period close and the financial statements.

close_statements.title: Accounts 7 — Period Close & Financial Statements
close_statements.desc: The period close and the financial statements in ZhiftERP: the freeze pair (Accounts Frozen Upto and the frozen-edit role) advanced by the nine-line checklist with the day-five target; cut-off through the Delivered/Received Items To Be Billed reports and the SRBNB age read; reading the Profit and Loss Statement, Balance Sheet, and Cash Flow reports with their filters and drill-downs; the Asset module from Asset Category and Is Fixed Asset capitalisation to automatic depreciation and the Sell/Scrap disposal flow; and year-end with the Period Closing Voucher and the collated audit file.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The monthly close in ZhiftERP
lessons.html:
This module covers the period close and the financial statements: the close checklist, the cut-off reports, the three statement reports and how to read them, the Asset module, and year-end with the Period Closing Voucher.

What closing a month means in the system. A month is closed when:

1. All its documents are submitted (cut-off — Chapter 3's reports find the stragglers).
2. The recurring Journal Entries have run and the month's journals are reviewed (module 2).
3. The standing checks have passed — reconciliations, bridges, ties (Chapter 2 lists them in order).
4. The Trial Balance has been scanned and its anomalies worked (module 1).
5. The period is locked: Accounts Settings > Accounts Frozen Upto is advanced to the month's end date, and the matching stock freeze (Stock Settings > Stock Frozen Upto) moves with it. From that moment, postings dated inside the sealed month are refused for everyone except the holders of the Role Allowed to Set Frozen Accounts & Edit Frozen Entries — a role granted to two named people at most (module 8).

A closed month's statements can be circulated without qualification, and they stay as reported: corrections discovered later post in the current month under module 2's rules.

Why monthly. Closing once a year produces the January backlog: twelve months of unsubmitted drafts, unswept suspense, unreconciled banks, and unaccrued costs, processed months after the events. Closing monthly keeps each month's work small because the previous month's was done, catches errors while the documents and the people are fresh, and turns year-end into an ordinary close plus a short annual list (Chapter 8). The first monthly close carries the backlog and takes days; the sixth takes hours. The standing target: day five — sealed and read by the fifth working day.

The three statement reports. All under Accounting > Financial Statements, all produced from the sealed month:

• Profit and Loss Statement — what the period earned and consumed (Chapter 4).
• Balance Sheet — what the business owns and owes at the sealed date (Chapter 5).
• Cash Flow — where the money went (Chapter 6).

All three share the same filters — Company, period, periodicity, Cost Center — and every figure drills to the General Ledger on click.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the close checklist. Chapter 3: cut-off and its reports. Chapters 4-6: reading the three statements. Chapter 7: the Asset module. Chapter 8: year-end, the audit, and the HealthTrade case. Chapter 9: review and the law.
